title: MiniMax Open-Sources MCode Stack: 15 Agent Skills Its Coding Team Uses Daily
abstract: MiniMax has open-sourced MCode Stack , the workflows and agent skills its team uses to build MiniMax Code. The MiniMax MCode Stack agent skills went public on October 28, 2026 under the MIT license . It is not a prompt collection. Each piece is a SKILL.md skill or checklist that installs directly into MiniMax Code . For developers, it turns harness engineering habits into steps an agent can actually run. We just open-sourced MCode Stack: the actual workflows and skills the MiniMax Code team uses every day to build MiniMax Code. https://t.co/vREt7i8m2M MCode Stack is an open-source repo of agent skills from MiniMax’s MiniMax Code team. MiniMax Code is the MiniMax’s open-source terminal coding agent, also MIT-licensed. The stack holds no MiniMax Code source code. It holds only workflows, skills and checklists. The repo pairs with a column called MCode Engineering Notes . Each note explains one idea. The repo makes that idea runnable. Published notes cover subagents , tool context , compaction versus memory and long bash commands . A note on per-turn context tax is marked upcoming. MiniMax’s stack ships 15 skills, grouped by moment in the working day: A few ideas stand out. independent-review gives the reviewer exactly 3 inputs: the diff, the requirement and test results. It deliberately withholds the author’s conversation. The reasoning: a reviewer inheriting the author’s context repeats the author’s blind spots. The 6 engineering-* skills are adapted from Google Engineering Practices . That material stays under CC-BY 3.0, per the stack’s NOTICE . There are 3 paths, per the README : The same catalog works in Claude Code with /plugin marketplace add MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack . MiniMax Code also reads ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/ . title: Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding
abstract: Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap . FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face , with vLLM and SGLang plugins . FlashMap is a speculative decoding drafter that maps Gaussian noise to a token block in 1 step. A small drafter proposes K tokens. The target model then checks all K in 1 parallel pass and keeps the longest matching prefix. Output stays exactly what the target would produce. Speed depends on 2 things. How many drafted tokens get accepted, and how cheaply they were drafted. EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively, so cost grows with block length. DFlash drafts the full block in 1 pass with block diffusion. DFlash predicts each slot in the block independently. The research team calls this the factorized approximation. Picture a continuation that is “new york” or “san diego” with equal odds. An independent drafter proposes “new diego” or “san york” half the time. The target rejects those at slot 2. FlashMap builds on Flow Map Language Models . Each noise sample maps to 1 full block. The noise picks the mode for every slot jointly. The drafter is a 6-block diffusion transformer (DiT), with embedding dimension 2048 and 16 attention heads. It reads hidden states from target layers 1, 9, 17, 25 and 33. Embedding matrix and LM head are copied from the target and stay frozen. Both drafters train on 500K samples from Open-PerfectBlend . Total compute across all models and ablations was about 4,600 GPU hours on H200s. The research team retrained EAGLE-3 and DFlash on the same data and settings. Tests cover 9 benchmarks across math, code and chat, at temperatures 0 and 1. A shuffle test checks whether drafts use real inter-token structure. At 2 steps, FlashMap recovers most of the joint-structure gain of a 16-step teacher. At 1 step, it keeps only a small fraction. Drafting 4 noise samples as a tree raised speedup by 11% on average. Average speedups are computed by Marktechpost from Figure 1(c) of the FlashMap paper. Matched rows use the authors’ retrained baselines. The flashmap package needs only torch and transformers>=4.56 . Install it with uv pip install flashmap . A spec_generate call runs drafter and target together on 1 GPU. For serving, the project page gives 2 paths: Set num_steps=2 to trade some speed for higher acceptance. For sampling above temperature 0, vLLM needs "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic" . title: Meet Google DeepMind’s Genie 4: Real-Time World Model With Native Audio
abstract: Google DeepMind has released Genie 4 as a research preview for trusted testers. The Genie 4 world model generates explorable worlds from text and image prompts in real time. It also generates the soundscape: ambient noise, music and character dialogue. Users move with keyboard controls and steer events with plain-language prompts. The bigger change is architectural. A Gemini model now runs inside the simulation loop as a planner. That pattern is important for anyone building training environments for agents or robots. Genie 4 is a world model from Google DeepMind that simulates interactive environments frame by frame. It is not a video clip generator. Each frame responds to user input as it arrives. DeepMind states that the model is natively multimodal . Audio, music and dialogue are generated together with the visuals. It is DeepMind’s first real-time world model to generate audio natively. It succeeds Genie 3 , announced in August 2025. Genie 3 ran at 720p and 24 frames per second, with visual memory reaching back 1 minute. Genie 4 borrows from 2 parts of the Gemini family. Gemini Omni anchors the look and behavior of each world. Other Gemini models handle the reasoning that keeps a simulation coherent. The runtime loop works like this: Between user inputs, Gemini also steers the scene so the world keeps progressing. DeepMind team frames this as an early step toward hybrid world models . In that design, a language model handles structure and narrative, while Genie renders pixels and sound. DeepMind released no benchmark tables for Genie 4. The comparison below uses only disclosed specs from each project’s own source. Genie 4 is live for trusted testers today. According to DeepMind, it is expected to be available soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie . Early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio come next. All Genie 4 video and audio will carry SynthID watermarks. DeepMind states that it ran internal safety evaluations before the preview. Testers so far span creative industries, journalism, education, gaming and engineering. title: Meet LEANN: An Open-Source Vector Index that Shrinks a 60M-Chunk RAG Index from 201 GB to 6 GB
abstract: UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab built LEANN , an open-source vector index that stores almost no embeddings. The LEANN vector index recomputes embeddings at query time instead of saving them to disk. The repo benchmark shows a 60 million chunk Wikipedia index dropping from 201 GB to 6 GB. The research paper won the Best Research Paper award at MLSys 2026 . So, it brings semantic search and RAG over personal data, on a laptop. LEANN is a low-storage approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index built on top of FAISS . It targets one problem: vector indexes are often bigger than the data they index. The research paper shows a 76 GB corpus needs 173 GB of embeddings plus a 15 GB HNSW graph. That more than doubles the raw data. LEANN keeps a pruned graph, drops the full vectors, and rebuilds them on demand. The code is MIT licensed and installs with uv pip install leann . Graph indexes like HNSW visit only a small set of nodes per query. LEANN exploits that. It stores the graph plus a compact product quantization (PQ) table. At query time, it re-embeds only nodes on the search path. 3 techniques keep this practical: In ablations, two-level search gives an average 1.4x speedup. Adding batching raises it to 1.8x. Embedding recomputation still accounts for about 76% of query latency. The research team tested NQ, TriviaQA, GPQA and HotpotQA against a 60M-passage RPJ-Wiki datastore. Latency is measured at 90% Recall@3. All figures below are self-reported in the research paper . On NQ, with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN and HNSW both reach 25.5% downstream accuracy. LEANN uses 4 GB of storage. HNSW uses 188 GB. BM25 scores 18.3%, and PQ compression scores 17.9%. The cost is search time. LEANN retrieval takes 2.48 s on NQ, versus 0.05 s for HNSW. Generation takes about 20 s, so end-to-end latency rises from 20.95 s to 23.34 s. Across datasets on the RTX 4090, LEANN retrieval ranges from 1.12 s (GPQA) to 7.12 s (HotpotQA). The IVF-based recomputation baseline, inspired by EdgeRAG , is up to 200x slower. LEANN improves exact match by up to 11.8% over BM25. The GitHub repo reports similar savings on personal data. 400K chat messages shrink from 1.8 GB to 64 MB. 38K browser entries shrink from 130 MB to 6.4 MB. Storage, latency and accuracy figures come from the LEANN paper v2 , Tables 1 and 2 and Section 7.2 (self-reported). License and design rows link to each project’s own source. The repo ships ready apps for documents, Apple Mail, Chrome history, WeChat, iMessage, and ChatGPT or Claude exports. MCP readers pull live data from Slack and Twitter bookmarks. LEANN also runs as a semantic search MCP server for Claude Code . On 30 SWE-Bench Pro tasks from ContextBench, the team reports 24.2% initial relevant-code recall versus 11.4% for BM25. The agent also used 8.4% fewer tokens. HNSW is the default backend, with DiskANN for faster search. Generation works with Ollama, Hugging Face, Anthropic, or any OpenAI-compatible API. It supports Ubuntu, Arch, WSL, macOS and Windows. Some apps, like Apple Mail search, are macOS only. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and PyPI package . title: Liquid AI Releases LFM3: 6 Open-Weight 2B-Class Multimodal Models
abstract: Liquid AI has released LFM3 , its new generation of Liquid Foundation Models. Liquid AI LFM3 is a family of 6 open-weight, 2B-class models built on one shared backbone. The family covers text, vision, audio, omni and decision tasks. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU. Developers can then deploy on phones, laptops, private servers or the cloud. LFM3 is a multimodal model family from Liquid AI that branches 6 models from 1 base. All of them start from LFM3-1.7B-Base . The backbone mixes 3 operators across 24 layers . There are 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention layers and 6 global attention layers. The SWA window is 256 tokens. Convolution kernels grew from 3 to 7. Liquid AI team found this mix with its hardware-in-the-loop architecture search. LFM2 was tuned on 1 phone and 1 laptop. LFM3 was tuned across 14 device and backend combinations. These include a Raspberry Pi 5 and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. Other changes include head-wise sigmoid gates on attention, partial RoPE on global layers and sandwich norm. The base model saw 22T tokens. The last 3.5T tokens were agent-heavy mid-training, which also extended context to 256K. Post-training ran in 4 stages. SFT on 1.75T tokens came first, then mixed RL. Next, 6 specialist teachers were distilled into 1 model, followed by agentic RL. Liquid AI reports that LFM3-1.7B beats LFM2.5-2.6B with 35% fewer parameters. The bigger story is the agent results. On WebArena-Verified it scores 38.42, against 28.94 for Qwen3.5-9B. On BFCL V4 it scores 71.39, against 62.83. Size still wins on knowledge and agentic coding. GPQA Diamond is 63.37, versus 80.40 for Qwen3.5-9B. SWE-bench Verified is 43.40, versus 51.20. Search narrows the gap: Humanity’s Last Exam rises from 7.17 to 13.90 with tools. Sources: Liquid LFM3 model card , MiniCPM5-2B card , Qwen3.5-4B card , Gemma 4 E4B card , LFM license . LFM3-VL-2B averages 71.4 across 62 vision benchmarks. Gemma 4 12B scores 71.7 on the same suite. It leads that comparison on visual grounding (77.3) and GUI understanding (83.1). Video (61.2) and agentic tasks (42.5) still trail larger API models. LFM3-Audio-2B reaches 6.2 English WER and a 3.8 UTMOSv2 TTS score. LFM3-Omni-2B scores 70.1 on Daily-Omni, against 61.3 for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B. d1-2B replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters. It improves Decision Bench from 83.6 to 85.2. Weights are on Hugging Face , the Liquid AI Playground and the Liquid API. The docs list GGUF, MLX and ONNX for the text and vision models. Runtimes include llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and Transformers. On-device, Liquid AI measured llama.cpp at Q4_0 with 32K context. A full 128K context needs 1.6 GB of KV cache. Qwen3.5-4B needs 4.3 GB. On 1 NVIDIA B300 with SGLang, LFM3-1.7B produces 3.6B tokens per day at 1,024 concurrent requests. Liquid AI also showed specialization. A few hours of SFT and GRPO on 1 A100 lifted wind-turbine defect classification to 67%. Check out the technical details , model weights and docs . title: Access Multiple AI Models in Your Python Apps Using OpenRouter
abstract: Access Multiple AI Models in Your Python Apps Using OpenRouter Learn how to get started with the OpenRouter API to call multiple AI models through one API, compare responses, switch models, and set up automatic fallbacks. By Bala Priya C , KDnuggets Contributing Editor & Technical Content Specialist on October 28, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Introduction Say you're building a support-ticket assistant, and you want to compare how GPT , Claude , and Llama each handle the same customer message before picking one. Normally that means signing up with three separate providers, learning three different authentication schemes, and rewriting your request code three times just to run one comparison. OpenRouter removes that repetition. It sits in front of dozens of providers and exposes them through a single API, so switching from one model to another is a one-line change instead of a new integration. Your Python code stays exactly the same regardless of which provider is actually answering the request. This article covers: Creating an OpenRouter account and getting an API key Sending your first request to a model with plain Python and requests Switching models by changing a single string, with no other code changes Letting OpenRouter pick a model automatically, and adding backup models for reliability We'll build this up one small script at a time, starting with the account setup. Prerequisites You don't need any AI or machine learning background to follow along. You do, however, need to be comfortable with basic Python, installing packages with pip , and setting an environment variable in your terminal. OpenRouter handles the model integration, so your code only sends text and reads the response. Creating an OpenRouter Account and API Key Go to OpenRouter and create a free account. Once you're signed in, open the Keys section from your account menu and generate a new API key. Give it a name you'll recognize later, like learning-key , and leave the other settings on their defaults. Copy the key somewhere safe. Store it as an environment variable so it never ends up committed to a repository by accident. On macOS or Linux: export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-key-here" TL;DR: Some models on OpenRouter are free to try, so you can follow this entire tutorial without adding a payment method. More on the why and how: OpenRouter marks certain models with a :free suffix; these route to fully free-to-use versions, with no payment method required. Every example in this tutorial uses one of these, so you can run all of it at zero cost. If a model ID in this tutorial stops responding by the time you read it, check the current list at openrouter.ai/models filtered to free, or swap in openrouter/free , which we'll cover below and which always resolves to whichever free model is currently available. Setting Up Your Project Create a folder for the project and a virtual environment inside it: mkdir support-bot-demo cd support-bot-demo python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate With the environment active, install requests . It is the only dependency you need. OpenRouter is a plain HTTP API, so there's no special software development kit (SDK) required to get started: pip install requests Note : OpenRouter does have an official SDK too. You can install openrouter with pip , which provides typed client objects instead of raw dictionaries. This tutorial only uses requests so every request stays visible as plain JSON, making it easier to see exactly what is being sent and received while you're still learning how the API is shaped. Once you get the hang of it, moving to the SDK later is a small change. Sending Your First Request to a Model Every request to OpenRouter looks the same regardless of which model answers it: a POST request to one endpoint, with your API key in the headers and a list of messages in the body. Here's a script that sends a customer support message to a model and prints the reply: import os import requests API_URL = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" API_KEY = os.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY") customer_message = ( "My order #48213 arrived with the wrong charger. " "I need the correct one before Friday, can you help?" ) payload = { "model": "meta-llama/llama-3.2-3b-instruct:free", "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise, polite customer support agent."}, {"role": "user", "content": customer_message}, ], } headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json", } response = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload) data = response.json() print(f"Model used: {data['model']}") print(f"Reply: {data['choices'][0]['message']['content']}") The payload dictionary is the entire request: model tells OpenRouter which model to use, written as provider/model-name , and messages follows the same role/content format you'd use with any chat-style model. The system message sets the tone once, and the user message is the actual ticket text. The response comes back as JSON, and the reply text is in data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] — the same shape you'd get from most chat completion APIs, since OpenRouter normalizes every provider's response into the same OpenAI-compatible format. Switching Models Without Changing Your Code Since the model is just a string in the payload, comparing providers means changing one line. Here's a small function that takes the model name as an argument, so you can call it with different models back to back: def ask_model(model_name, message): payload = { "model": model_name, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise, polite customer support agent."}, {"role": "user", "content": message}, ], } response = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload) return response.json() ticket = "My order #48213 arrived with the wrong charger. I need the correct one before Friday." for model in ["meta-llama/llama-3.2-3b-instruct:free", "qwen/qwen3-4b:free", "mistralai/mistral-7b-instruct:free"]: result = ask_model(model, ticket) reply = result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] print(f"--- {model} ---") print(reply, "\n") ask_model is the same request logic from the first script (it reuses API_URL and headers from there), only wrapped so model_name is a parameter instead of a hardcoded value. The loop calls it three times with three different models and prints each reply next to the model that produced it. This is the core benefit of OpenRouter in practice: you're calling one function three times instead of working with three different APIs. Letting OpenRouter Pick a Free Model for You Sometimes you don't care which specific model answers; you just want a working reply without picking one yourself, and without any risk of a paid model slipping in. Setting model to openrouter/free hands that decision to OpenRouter's Free Models Router , which always selects from currently available free models: payload = { "model": "openrouter/free", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": ticket}], } response = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload) data = response.json() print(f"OpenRouter picked: {data['model']}") This is the safest default for prototyping: no matter which free model happens to be available that day, you're never charged. It's a different setting from openrouter/auto , which picks whatever model best fits the prompt and can include paid ones. Separately, when you do specify a model by name, OpenRouter often has more than one provider hosting it, and you can choose which one it uses with a provider field. For example, set payload["provider"] = {"sort": "price"} to favor the cheapest provider, or {"sort": "latency"} to favor the fastest one. This matters most once you're working with paid models at real volume; it has little effect on :free models, since there's no per-token cost to optimize against in the first place.

title: Can This Open-Source Model Beat AI Detectors? Let’s Test It Locally
abstract: Can This Open-Source Model Beat AI Detectors? Let’s Test It Locally Can a free, open-source AI humanizer beat paid tools? We tested a 12B model locally and compared the results against AI detectors to see if the hype is real. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 28, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence You do not need to pay for an expensive subscription to rewrite AI-generated content anymore. Open-source models like Humanizer let you do it locally, without monthly fees, API costs, or sending your writing to a third-party service. The model is gaining attention in the open-source community, with more than 143,000 downloads and 2,100 likes reported on Hugging Face in early October 2026. Its developer also claims that 95% of 210 rewritten English drafts were classified as human-written by Originality.ai , although that result has not been independently verified. Screenshot from jialinyyzz/humanizer In this tutorial, we will download the 12-billion-parameter Humanizer model, run it locally on a Linux machine using llama.cpp with NVIDIA CUDA support, and use it to rewrite AI-generated text. We will then test the results against popular AI detectors, including Originality.ai, GPTZero , and Copyleaks , to see whether this free, open-source alternative can actually deliver on its claims. Understanding the Humanizer Model Humanizer is an open-source, 12-billion-parameter model built on Google's Gemma 4 12B . Unlike general-purpose language models, it is specifically fine-tuned to rewrite AI-generated content into more natural, human-like writing while preserving the original meaning, facts, and important details. Image from jialinyyzz/humanizer · Hugging Face The model was trained on 28,598 pairs of AI-generated drafts and real human-written text , collected from sources such as academic papers, government reports, emails, Reddit, and Hacker News. It first learned to transform AI-written drafts into human-like text through supervised fine-tuning. The developers then used Direct Preference Optimization with 3,918 preference pairs, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization , where a large language model (LLM) judge evaluated rewrites for factual accuracy, unnecessary copying, and changes in meaning. When you provide a draft, Humanizer rewrites the wording, adjusts sentence structure, removes repetitive AI-style phrasing, and varies sentence length while trying to keep the original information intact. Interestingly, the developers did not use AI detectors during training . Instead, they focused on improving writing quality and factual consistency. According to the developer's evaluation, 95% of 210 English rewrites were classified as human-written by Originality.ai , while the quantized Q8_0 version achieved approximately 93%. These results are developer-reported, and the model can still introduce factual errors or perform differently across detectors. You can also download the desktop application for Windows and macOS and run it offline without writing any code. For advanced users, Humanizer supports llama.cpp, Ollama , Transformers , MLX , and vLLM . In this tutorial, we will run the Q8_0 model locally on Linux using llama.cpp with NVIDIA CUDA support. 1. Install llama-server with CUDA First, we need to set up llama.cpp, an open-source inference engine that lets us run LLMs locally without relying on cloud APIs. We will use its llama-server component to serve Humanizer through a local HTTP API. Since our Linux machine already has NVIDIA CUDA installed, we can build llama.cpp with GPU acceleration to make text generation faster. Clone the llama.cpp repository and build the server with CUDA support: git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp cd llama.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON cmake --build build --config Release --target llama-server -j Once the build is complete, verify the installation: ./build/bin/llama-server --version Output: built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64 2. Download and Run Humanizer Next, we will download the 8-bit quantized version of Humanizer from Hugging Face. Quantization reduces the model's memory requirements, making it easier to run on consumer GPUs without loading the full-precision weights. We will use the Q8_0 version, which offers a good balance between model quality and memory usage, and then launch it using llama-server . Install the Hugging Face CLI: pip install -U huggingface_hub Download the model weights and prompt configuration: hf download jialinyyzz/humanizer \ humanizer-12b-Q8_0.gguf prompt_format.json \ --local-dir ./humanizer-model The Q8_0 model requires substantial GPU memory. If your GPU has less VRAM available, you can try the smaller humanizer-12b-Q6_K.gguf version instead. Start the server: ./build/bin/llama-server \ -m ./humanizer-model/humanizer-12b-Q8_0.gguf \ -c 8192 \ -np 1 \ -ngl 99 \ -fa on \ -b 2048 \ -ub 512 \ -t 8 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8910 Here, -ngl 99 offloads all model layers to the GPU, -c 8192 sets the context window, and -fa on enables Flash Attention. The server runs on port 8910 and is accessible only from the local machine. Open another terminal and check whether the model is available: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8910/models If the server returns the loaded model information, Humanizer is ready to accept requests. 3. Rewrite AI-Generated Text Now that Humanizer is running locally, we can test it on AI-generated content. We will create a short article, send it to the model through the local API, and save the rewritten version to a text file. The model uses a specific prompt format to guide the rewriting process, so we will load the official configuration rather than writing our own instructions. First, create a file called draft.txt and add an AI-generated article of around 200 words. For this experiment, we used an article about running AI models locally, which GPTZero flagged as 100% AI-generated, as shown in the screenshot below. Next, create a Python file called humanize.py : import json import urllib.request # Load prompt and article pf = json.load(open("humanizer-model/prompt_format.json")) draft = open("draft.txt").read().strip() # Model settings body = { "prompt": pf["instr"] + "\n\n" + draft + pf["sep"], "temperature": 1.0, "top_p": 0.95, "top_k": 0, "min_p": 0, "repeat_penalty": 1.0, "n_predict": 2048, "seed": -1, } # Generate humanized text req = urllib.request.Request( "http://127.0.0.1:8910/completion", json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"}, ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600) as response: result = json.load(response)["content"].strip() # Save output with open("humanized.txt", "w") as f: f.write(result) print(result) The script loads the original draft, combines it with the model's recommended instructions, and sends it to the local llama-server . We use a temperature of 1.0 and a top_p of 0.95 , following the developer's recommended generation settings. The rewritten text is then saved automatically. Run the script: python3 humanize.py The rewritten article will appear in your terminal and will also be saved as humanized.txt . We then tested the rewritten article using GPTZero, and the results were quite promising. The AI detection score dropped from 100% to 49%, while the human-written score increased to 51%. GPTZero was uncertain about the text but indicated that it would likely be considered human-written. This shows a noticeable improvement after running the article through Humanizer, although results may vary with different content and detectors. Final Thoughts After testing Humanizer on multiple AI-generated articles, I found the results to be quite hit or miss. Sometimes, the rewritten content was classified as human-written, while other times, detectors still flagged it as AI-generated. Based on my testing, it felt like a 50-50 chance of getting a good result. I am not entirely sure why the results were so inconsistent.

title: Which Local LMs are Best For Which Tasks
abstract: Which Local LMs are Best For Which Tasks A local language model is one whose actual weights, the enormous file of learned numbers that constitutes the trained model, you download and run entirely on your own hardware. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 28, 2026 in Language Models Someone spends an evening reading "best local LLM" roundups, settles on whichever name keeps showing up at the top, downloads it, and points it at the thing they actually needed help with that week, say, cleaning up a Python script. But it's mediocre at that. Not broken, just unimpressive, in the specific way a generalist is unimpressive at a specialist's job. The model wasn't bad. It was never a coding model to begin with, and nothing in the roundup that recommended it ever said so. That mismatch is the entire reason this guide exists. "Best" was never a single ranking, and treating it like one is how a genuinely capable model ends up feeling disappointing for no fault of its own. This article works the other way around: what a local language model actually is, why running one on your own hardware is worth doing at all, and then, model by model, with real cited proof rather than vibes, exactly what each one is good at. It closes with one table built specifically to answer the only question that actually matters: for the task in front of you right now, which model should you reach for? What Is a Language Model, and What Makes One "Local"? A language model is, at its core, a system trained to predict text: given everything that came before it in a conversation or a document, what's the most plausible next piece of text? That simple mechanism, applied at enormous scale, is what lets a model answer questions, write code, summarize a document, or hold a conversation. Every well-known AI chat product, whether it's ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, is built on top of a language model doing exactly this. " Local " describes something about how you access that model, not what it is. A local language model is one whose actual weights, the enormous file of learned numbers that constitutes the trained model, you download and run entirely on your own hardware. No API call leaves your machine. No account is required to use it. No company's server ever sees your prompt. That's a genuinely different relationship to the technology than using a hosted model through a website or an API key, where every request travels to someone else's infrastructure and the model itself is something you can query but never actually possess. Why Local Language Models Actually Matter Privacy is the most obvious one: if nothing about a prompt ever leaves your device, there's no third party in a position to log, train on, or leak it, which matters directly for anything involving client data, medical information, unpublished work, or a company's internal documents Cost is the second, since once the weights are on disk, there's no per-token bill accumulating with every request, which changes the calculus entirely for anything high-volume or experimental Offline capability is the third, genuinely useful for fieldwork, air-gapped environments, or just an unreliable connection Control is the fourth and most underrated: a local model doesn't get silently swapped, deprecated, or have its behavior changed by a provider's update; it behaves the same way today as it will in a year, because you're the one holding the weights Ollama , the tool that's become the de facto standard for running these models locally, hosts a public library of ready-to-pull GGUF builds for every model covered in this article, and the real download numbers behind some of these models, covered in detail later in this piece, run into the tens of millions. Why "Best" Depends on the Task, Not the Leaderboard This is the idea the rest of the article is built around, so it's worth making explicit. A single aggregate benchmark score, or a raw parameter count, tells you surprisingly little about whether a specific model will actually serve you well on a specific task. A model can score well on general knowledge and still write mediocre code. A small, efficient model can lead its entire weight class on tool calling while trailing badly on creative writing. Treating any one number as "the" ranking is how people end up disappointed by genuinely good models used for the wrong job. It helps to know, briefly, what the benchmarks that show up throughout this article are actually measuring, since they're not interchangeable. Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) tests broad general knowledge across dozens of academic subjects, a reasonable proxy for how much a model "knows." HumanEval specifically tests whether a model can write correct, functioning code for a given problem, a direct measure of coding capability rather than general intelligence. MT-Bench measures how well a model follows instructions and holds a coherent multi-turn conversation, closer to what " feels good to actually talk to " captures. Keep those distinctions in mind as the numbers show up model by model below, since a model leading on one says nothing certain about where it lands on the others. The Models, One at a Time Seven models make up this article: six general-purpose chat models plus one embedding model that plays a different but essential role in any local retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setup. Every claim below is checked against the model's own official card or a cited independent benchmark, not repeated secondhand. 1. Phi-4-mini Phi-4-mini is Microsoft's answer to a specific question: how much real capability can you fit into a genuinely small model? Per Microsoft's own Phi-4-Mini Technical Report , it scores 67.3 on MMLU (5-shot) and 70.4 on BigBench-Hard, competitive numbers for a model roughly a fifth the size of many 20B-class competitors. A separate, independent 2026 evaluation of reasoning consistency across foundation models found Phi-4-mini leading its comparison group on step-by-step reasoning accuracy specifically, per a cross-platform reasoning capabilities study . That's a meaningfully different claim than just "knows a lot of facts"; it suggests the model's actual reasoning process holds together reliably even at this size. What it's exceptionally good at: Lightweight general question-answering Structured output and function calling It's the model worth reaching for when the constraint is the hardware itself, not the ambition of the task 2. Gemma 4 E2B and E4B Gemma 4 is Google DeepMind's current generation of open-weight models, released April 2, 2026, and verified directly from Google's own model card . The E2B and E4B variants are the two smallest in a five-size family. They are natively multimodal, accepting text, images, and, on these smaller variants specifically, audio too. Both carry native function-calling support trained directly into the model weights rather than bolted on through prompting, and a 128K context window even at this small size. What it's exceptionally good at: Writing and document-focused work, where its multimodal input and clean instruction adherence show up directly in output quality, and genuinely constrained edge deployment, since the E2B variant's footprint is small enough to run on phones and other genuinely limited devices 3. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct posts 74.2 on MMLU and 84.8 on HumanEval according to Qwen's own technical release notes , genuinely strong numbers on both general knowledge and coding for a 7B model. The dedicated coding variant, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct , pushes further still, reaching 88.4 on HumanEval in independently logged evaluation results, a real jump over the general-purpose version specifically on code generation.

title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
abstract: Chapter 01 : Science funders and societies We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program , which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects. We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.) Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems. Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute , a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours. We’re sharing how this program has further scaled up from supporting individual scientists to developing a large number of scientific partnerships with institutions and foundations to support researchers across many scientific fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries. Science funders and societies Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research: The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics. The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute. Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program. Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science. The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities. CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS Registry®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances. Institutions Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery: Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide. Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development. The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease. Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience. EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC. Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases. Research projects and initiatives As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are: FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior. LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land. AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs. gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis. Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof. Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis. What’s next Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery.

title: Expanding our partnership with GSA to bring Claude to all levels of government
abstract: We are expanding our partnership with the General Services Administration (GSA) through a new agreement that gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, and the Claude API. For the first time, the discount applies across every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months. The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments. We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks. Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment. The discounts offered through the agreement are estimated to save the government $1 billion. Agencies are not bound by a minimum spend commitment and will be able to pay for the usage they consume. How Claude is helping public servants get more done Government agencies are using Claude to solve some of their most important challenges. Examples include managing backlogs, records and forms, and modernizing old code. Some of the ways agencies are using Claude include: Utah gave Claude Code to 34 developers across 10 state agencies. 80% had a working environment within 30 minutes, 71% reported saving 20+ hours by the end of the four-week pilot. A US state CIO confirmed their team was able to respond to a ransomware attack in 8 minutes vs. the usual 2-3 days thanks to Claude. A US federal security team used Claude Mythos to detect and patch the vulnerability that would have allowed for the takeover of a critical production system in about two days. A human penetration test the month before had missed it. A cybersecurity professional at a major agency found and patched bugs in critical financial systems. A US state IT developer moved nearly 900 API methods to a new framework in two days. The project had been scoped for a month. A US state IT director used Claude Code to document 12 legacy code repositories, mapping 467 database tables and flagging 27 risks along the way. More than half of the US states, some of the largest localities, and some of the countries largest critical infrastructure operators participated in our SLTT cyber defense program. Meeting government security requirements Agencies can use Claude for their most sensitive unclassified work. Claude for Government, which delivers Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities and provides near-feature parity with commercial offerings at a FedRAMP High authorization level, was made generally available on September 30. Agencies building their own tools can use Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Vertex AI. On Bedrock, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High, with select models authorized for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads in AWS GovCloud. On Vertex AI, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High. Claude Enterprise is in process for FedRAMP Moderate authorization through the FedRAMP 20x program, marking the next evolution of how we are bringing the same innovative technology available commercially to the government. Getting started Government agencies can buy Claude at the OneGov discount through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule today. Whether your department or agency already uses Claude or is interested in using it, our Public Sector team will help discuss your options. For more information, contact us here .

title: Smart reports, surveys, and pooled group budgets for Claude Enterprise
abstract: Smart reports show what that work is, and where that work is happening, in-app surveys capture their feedback about how Claude is enabling them to do new work, and pooled group budgets let admins set one shared budget per team. All three are now generally available for Claude Enterprise. Smart reports show how your teams work in Claude, and how to spread what’s working Smart reports surface what a team gets done with Claude, and what that work costs. The reports show ambitious work your teams are doing with Claude, and how Claude made it possible. They then show how to turn that work into repeatable workflows, so the rest of your organization can do it too. Pick a team, a date range, and the products to include. Claude analyzes a sample of the team’s transcripts and groups the work into workstreams. See the spend for each one, the deliverables produced, and the most common points of friction, such as a missing connector or a failed tool call. Each report has one consolidated list of recommendations, including recurring workflows to turn into skills and rules to add to your code repository. Share any finding as an artifact with the people who can act on it. Reports also answer custom questions about model usage and cost, and admins can save their questions and custom insights as templates to reuse in future reports. If a spend limit is holding someone back, admins with billing permission can raise it from the report. Owners can let team leads who aren’t admins run reports for their own groups, so the people closest to the work act on the findings. Smart reports help admins understand adoption and inform investment planning, but they aren’t for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions. “We use smart reports across several initiatives. They give our applied AI team a grounded view of how Claude is being used across the company, which helps us prioritize what to do next and drive greater impact.” Keren Koshman, Head of Applied AI “Claude smart reports give us a new level of visibility into how AI is actually being used across our organization.
