title: 做能源與算力的“搭橋人”：達卯科技以能源大腦定義算電協同 | CPE 2026
abstract: 做能源與算力的“搭橋人”：達卯科技以能源大腦定義算電協同 | CPE 2026 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-27 15:44:41 來源： 量子位 破解綠電直連專案落地僵局 10月26日，2026國際算電協同產業鏈展覽會（CPE 2026）在上海世博展覽館開幕。達卯科技攜全棧算電協同技術產品體系亮相，全景呈現AI能源大模型和智慧體叢集應用、算電協同2.0平臺、預測-排程-交易核心功能引擎、智慧運營運維一體化管理平臺等。 達卯科技CEO簡煜忞受邀出席主論壇，發表《以能源大腦定義算電協同，構築AI算力與綠色能源融合新範式》主題演講，指出綠電直連的破局關鍵不在電能量淨值的零和博弈，而在多市場融合套利，並給出能源AI的系統解題路徑；達卯還率先提出E-AIDC能源驅動型智算中心新範式，展現算電協同產業鏈核心企業的認知高度與解題能力。 做能源與算力的“搭橋人”，破解綠電直連專案落地僵局 綠電直連是算電協同典型落地場景，卻長期卡在簽約環節。全國已批覆綠電直連專案數百個，真正開工落地的仍是少數。 簡煜忞在演講中指出，核心癥結在於發電方與算力方只圍繞電能量淨值討價還價，為“2毛6還是2毛8”的電價僵持半年；加之自發綠電大發時段與市場低價時段重合、容量電費又難以削減，單靠電量淨值雙方始終談不攏，幾分錢、幾釐錢的價差讓專案陷入零和博弈。 達卯科技的解法，是跳出電能量淨值博弈，從電能量、調節性、容量、碳四重市場融合尋優，先把蛋糕做大、再合理分配。 例如：在電能量價差空間，在佔電費五至六成的基礎電量之外，通過儲能削峰填谷、自發綠電與市場化購電的AI即時套利，壓低電量成本；容量電費正隨監管週期改革上漲，在容量輸配空間，以AI管控負荷側容量佔用，可顯著壓降輸配電成本，同時減輕對電網的容量佔用；在調節與碳收益空間，讓資料中心負荷參與需求響應、輔助服務獲取單次較高收益，並通過電能質量治理、綠電消納獲得獎勵性補貼與碳資產增值。 在西部某省專案中，達卯科技基於真實資料以能源大模型進行模擬，完成12000種場景、20個開放邊界的測算（相當於傳統20億次靜態場景計算），挖掘出3分以上的綜合價值空間，既填平雙方2分錢的認知價差，又留有最佳化餘量，最終實現投資方IRR提升約 20%、使用者到戶電價下降10%。 這一解法背後，是達卯全棧算電協同技術產品體系與運維運營一體化服務能力的雙重支撐。 依託自研垂類能源大模型與原子智慧體、場景化智慧體叢集構建的“融合推演智慧+ 統籌博弈智慧”雙引擎，實現負荷、發電、電價等多源時空、多市場資料預測和趨勢感知，以及電能量、調節、容量、碳多重市場全域性統籌、多目標最佳策略求解，構建智算中心能源運營全鏈路能力閉環；面向未來，針對電力市場政策頻繁迭代的不確定性，原子智慧體以通用、可靈活編排的能力適配各地規則差異，實現“一套系統落地、一套服務交付”，並可平滑複用至各類場景。 從IDC到AIDC，再到E-AIDC，“能源”定義下一代智算中心 Gartner 2026年預測，Agentic時代智慧體單任務token消耗量可達標準GenAI的5-30倍，算力需求指數級攀升，GW級智算中心將走向普及。 80%綠電消納成為國家樞紐節點新建資料中心的合規門檻，能耗指標與電網接入條件成為專案落地的現實前提，算電協同已從成本最佳化的可選項，轉變為安全落地的必選項，能源問題成為算力擴張的核心約束。 在這一趨勢下，資料中心形態正經歷第三級演進：傳統IDC以風火水電的基建思維建設，AIDC轉向算力驅動，而E-AIDC迴歸“能源效率”本源——新一代Token工廠，首先是一項“能源工程”，其次才是一項“資料中心工程”。 達卯科技率先提出E-AIDC（Energy-driven AI Data Center，能源驅動型智算中心）產業概念，並從三個維度給出框架：Energy能源運營，以全生命週期運營替代一次性建設思維；Eco低碳高效，以電算一體、源網荷儲協同重構能效與碳效；Electricity綠電直連，讓綠電消納成為專案落地的合規前提，成為新一代Token工廠穿越週期的長期競爭力。 其核心，是把資料中心打造成與電網主動互動、主動調節的自最佳化系統，實現可預測、可調節、可最佳化、可增值，並通過調節性資源參與全市場交易釋放價值。 這正是達卯科技以能源大腦定義算電協同，為新一代Token工廠構築長期穩定的能源核心競爭力。 CPE 2026火熱進行中，展期至10月28日下午14:00，達卯科技世博展覽館H3館E1010展位恭候各界蒞臨，共探E-AIDC時代的算電協同機遇。 title: OXR強勢開源！1.3B橫掃全球三榜第一，速度快過Paddle、MinerU，RSI讓它卷出新高度
abstract: OXR強勢開源！1.3B橫掃全球三榜第一，速度快過Paddle、MinerU，RSI讓它卷出新高度 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-27 15:41:02 來源： 量子位 開源一週，Github 拿下超 1000 star，X上關注度破百萬，並登上 Today‘s news 推薦 文件解析賽道，又迎來一位強勁的新選手。 OXR 正式開源：主模型僅 1.3B 參數，在 OmniDocBench、olmOCR-Bench 和 DocParsingBench 三項基準測試中全部登頂，完整解析速度也超過了同場參測的 PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 和 MinerU2.5-Pro，把輕量模型的精度與效率同時推到了榜首。 其背後的 SoMark 團隊來自國內一家初創公司，深耕於文件智慧領域，此前持續圍繞核心產品 SoMark 打磨解析能力，如今推出了開源模型 OXR。 OXR 的全稱是 Optical Everything Recognition ，從 OCR 到 OXR，OXR 要處理的遠不止文字。它能夠解析表格、公式、化學式等 13 類文件元素，準確還原多欄版面的閱讀順序，輸出 Markdown / JSON，並保留版面座標，讓複雜文件成為 Agent 可以繼續使用的資料。 1 高精度解析，全球三榜第一 根據團隊公佈的評測結果， OXR 在 OmniDocBench、olmOCR-Bench 和 DocParsingBench 上分別取得 97.18、87.84 和 87.76 分，均位列第一。 分數之外，更直觀的是看 OXR 如何處理複雜文件。 一張跨行跨列的表格，文字識別正確只是第一步。行列關係或合併單元格一旦錯位，數字就可能對應到錯誤的專案。OXR 可以保留這些結構，並將表格輸出為 HTML，供後續展示和處理。 科研文件裡的難點則更密集：數學公式有上下標和巢狀結構，化學內容還有反應式與分子結構圖。OXR 將公式輸出為 LaTeX，化學方程式用 mhchem 表示，化學結構式用 SMILES 表示，讓這些內容從頁面上的圖形變成可繼續處理的表達。 多欄論文、報紙和試卷還考驗閱讀順序。即便每個區域都識別正確，左右欄串讀、正文與旁註混雜，仍會破壞原文含義。OXR 在識別內容的同時判斷閱讀順序，並提供版面座標，保留內容在頁面中的位置。 這些能力共同構成了 OXR 的“Everything”：覆蓋文字、表格、公式、化學結構式、程式碼塊等 13 類文件元素，將 PDF 和文件圖片解析為 Markdown / JSON，供 Agent、RAG 等下游流程使用。 2 精度與速度雙 SOTA：不只準，而且快 處理單份文件，幾秒的差異未必明顯；當任務變成批次論文入庫、檔案整理或研報解析，處理效率就會直接影響等待時間與算力佔用。 根據團隊公佈的同條件完整解析測試結果，在同一張 RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell（96GB）顯示卡上，解析從 OmniDocBench 隨機抽取的 100 頁文件， OXR 平均用時約 101 秒，PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 和 MinerU2.5-Pro 則分別需要約 145 秒和 255 秒。 小參數、高精度、快速度，這次出現在了同一個模型上。 這得益於OXR 在任務分工上做的一個巧妙設計： 由輕量版面分析模型定位內容區域，再由主模型完成內容識別與閱讀順序判斷。 把排序併入內容識別階段，減少了單獨處理閱讀順序的額外開銷，也讓模型能夠結合內容語義判斷先後關係。這是 OXR 兼顧解析質量與效率 的一項架構設計。 3 RSI：圍繞錯樣本和弱樣本持續改進 耀眼的成績背後，OXR 的訓練思路同樣值得看。我們都知道，文件解析很難靠一套固定樣本覆蓋所有問題。場景、語言、版式不斷變化，如何讓模型面對沒見過的複雜文件，也能穩定輸出可靠的解析結果呢？ OXR 創新性地 在後訓練階段首次引入面向文件解析的遞迴自我改進（Recursive Self-Improvement，RSI） 訓練範式，將解析中的錯樣本和弱樣本轉化為下一輪訓練的依據。 這套流程可以理解為一次由多個 AI 模型協作完成的“查錯與補課”： OXR 先解析無標籤文件，產生待評估的結果。 外部模型評判結果、逐樣本分析錯誤原因，獨立聚類模型將問題按原因歸類。 外部模型圍繞這些問題定向生成訓練資料，用於下一輪 OXR 訓練。 這樣一來，訓練資料的準備就有了明確的問題指向：模型哪裡薄弱，就圍繞哪裡補充資料，加快了模型迭代的步伐。同時， 閉環中新增加的訓練資料無需人工標註， 也突破了人工準備材料帶來的效率瓶頸。 4 版面分析可插拔，業務適配更靈活 模型讀錯了，需要提高準確率；但很多時候，解析結果不符合預期，是因為業務對文件結構有不同的定義。 例如，同一組圖片，資料歸檔可能希望整體保留，圖片檢索則需要逐張提取；一個包含標題、文字和邊框的區域，有的業務按文本拆分，有的業務希望整體作為表格處理。兩種需求都可能合理。 對此，OXR 將版面分析設計為獨立、可插拔模組。 你可以直接使用內建版面分析模型，也可以接入符合自身業務標準的其他版面分析模型，調整元素類別、區域邊界與內容分組，再繼續複用 OXR 的內容識別和閱讀順序判斷能力。 對於構建 RAG、Agent 和文件工作流的開發者，OXR 無疑提供了一個兼顧解析精度、處理速度與版面適配能力的開源選擇。 目前，OXR 已開放程式碼與模型權重，並提供線上 Demo 和免費 API，方便開發者直接用真實文件檢驗效果： GitHub 程式碼倉庫：https://github.com/SoMarkAI/OXR Hugging Face 模型權重：https://huggingface.co/SoMarkAI/OXR-1.0 線上 Demo：https://free-oxr.somark.cn/ 免費 API：https://free-oxr.somark.cn/api/v1 有更多生產級文件解析需求的團隊，也可以瞭解同一團隊打造、由獨立模型驅動的文件解析引擎 SoMark。 SoMark 官網：https://somark.cn/ 從 SoMark 到 OXR，這支團隊向開發者開放他們在長期探索與實踐中積累的寶貴經驗，正傳達了他們的價值取向：讓文件中的知識成為 AI 可用的高質量資料，進入更多真實業務場景。 title: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
abstract: Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. Posted in:

title: Voice Agents are here. Context turns them into real customer value.
abstract: *Voice is already changing how customers interact with brands. People who moved from storefronts to websites to apps now expect to simply talk to the companies they buy from, and the same shift is reaching suppliers, drivers, and field teams. *Most enterprise AI so far has faced inward. The larger opportunity is in the conversations companies have with customers and partners every day, and each of those conversations can now be captured, understood, and acted on in real time. *Any team can build a voice agent that talks back, but value is created only when the agent has context on who is calling. From there, it can adapt to that person, stay within set rules, and get better with every call. *On Databricks, the agent's brain sits next to your governed data. Context and ontology ground every answer, fast AI decisions tailor each turn, and every call feeds a learning loop. *Getting started is straightforward. Pick one high-volume routine call, measure how well the agent handles it, and use the DIVA blueprint as the starting point for the next one. Before you read further: watch this short demo . In this short demo, the voice agent makes a decision in a fraction of a second, partway through the call, and changes how it responds without interrupting the conversation. That same real-time decision making lets a voice agent switch languages, hand a caller to a person at the right moment, or give your most valuable customers the experience they expect. Consider three moments that happen every day in consumer businesses: In each of these moments, voice is the fastest or only way the customer can reach the business. So if voice ultimately serves the customer and business need most effectively, why is it so often not available or, in more recent times, executed poorly? For years, the answer was that voice was too hard to get right. That is no longer true. Synthetic voices now sound natural, a conversation can be turned into text and acted on while the caller is still on the line, and today's voice agents can keep pace with the roughly 200 milliseconds it typically takes people to answer each other in conversation. What has not caught up is how most companies think about it. Enterprise AI investment has largely faced inward, toward assistants for employees, while the larger opportunity sits in the conversations companies have with customers and partners every day. One of the largest quick-service restaurant brands in the United States is already building toward exactly that, with a voice agent that lets guests add items to their cart, change their order, and check out simply by talking. Example use cases where voice agents can create value. Every one of these calls, from the driver moving a dock appointment to the traveler holding a room after a storm, depends on more than understanding speech. To be useful, the agent needs the same context your best employee would have: who is calling, what is already in motion for them, and what it is allowed to do about it. Most voice agent pilots prove that an agent can hold a conversation. Far fewer prove that it can be trusted with a real customer. Context closes that gap. With it, the agent can adapt to each caller, stay within your rules about what it can see and say, and get better with every call. Without it, even the most natural voice can only give generic answers. Consider a single call. A loyal customer phones about a late order. The agent already knows who they are, what they ordered, and where the package is. It apologizes, offers a loyalty credit it is authorized to give, and arranges a replacement. If the customer is still frustrated, the agent picks up on it in the moment and decides, in a fraction of a second, to route the call to the next available person. That person picks up with the full context, so the customer neither waits in a queue nor repeats themselves. The same pattern holds when a patient moves an appointment or a subscriber cannot log in after a charge they don't recognize. In each case, the agent picks up when the customer steps away from the app or website and needs an answer now, then hands them back to that same journey when the call is done. Pulling that context together on a live call is the real challenge. It lives across many systems, the agent needs it in a fraction of a second, and it has to stay governed the whole time. That is where Databricks comes in. A voice agent has two parts. The first is the conversation layer , which handles the call itself: carrying the audio, turning speech into text, and speaking the reply. Specialist partners do this well. In our prototype, LiveKit carries the call, Deepgram handles speech-to-text and the default voice, and ElevenLabs adds expressive voices. Phone carriers such as Twilio can bring in regular phone lines. The second part is the brain , which Databricks provides. On every turn of the call, it looks up the caller’s context, applies your business rules, and chooses the next step, whether that means answering a question, making an offer, or handing the call to a person. It also records each decision so your teams can review it later. The conversation layer shapes how the agent sounds. The brain decides whether it gets the answer right. The brain stands on a foundation of three things that already live together on Databricks. For Databricks customers, there is no new platform to stand up. The agent runs where your data already lives and connects to the systems you already run, such as ordering, loyalty, and CRM, through approved, read-only lookups. During a customer interaction, the agent uses your context and ontology to look up this person’s orders, your policies, and your product information, so every answer reflects your business rather than general knowledge from the internet. The agent only sees the records that belong to the caller, and it confirms who they are by checking your systems rather than taking their word for it. Your business decides which offers the agent can make, how much credit it can give, and the point at which a person takes over. If the agent cannot find the answer in your data, it tells the caller so and transfers them to a person rather than guessing. Every answer it does give can be traced back to the record it came from. Sensitive topics, such as medical, financial, or safety questions, are routed to a human by design, and the agent is built never to give medical advice. Only the conversation passes through speech partners, and customer data stays on your governed platform. A voice agent needs two kinds of thinking. Some decisions have to happen in a fraction of a second, like whether a driver with a dock problem or an upset caller should go to a person right now. Others need careful reasoning, like working out the right fix for a delayed order. Researchers call this fast and slow thinking , or System 1 and System 2, and AI is now being built the same way. Large language models (System 2) do the careful reasoning, while a new class of fast decision models (System 1), such as Jev from TypeSafe AI , handles the quick calls. Databricks brings System 1 decision making to your governed data with ai_decide , so the agent can make a quick call and show how confident it is. In a voice agent, the two work side by side on every turn of the conversation. This lets you use your most capable models where they make a real difference to the customer, and faster, lower-cost models for everything else. Every one of those decisions is recorded. With caller consent and recording disclosure handled at the phone layer, each call can be captured in one governed place: what was said, what was looked up, which model answered, and why each decision was made. Your teams control who can access those records and how long they are kept, using the same policies that already govern the rest of your data.

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
abstract: It's almost like Google's got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year. Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon . This isn't the Flash model equivalent we've been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while. Stop me if you've heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. It's so capable, in fact, that Google can't let you use it just yet. Gemini 4 Carbon reportedly makes big gains in cybersecurity applications. Google says the model shows a "significant leap" in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon. Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating "high-quality" patches compared to non-Google models. Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.

title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
abstract: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources. When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response: "To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)." My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.

title: "No human at the helm": Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
abstract: A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms’ human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday. Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee “seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC).” Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. “We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives,” Comer’s letter said. Comer suggested he may propose a federal law that would limit states’ regulatory authority. He said the committee’s probe of Delaware’s plan would “inform possible federal legislative efforts including proposals to appropriately limit state AI regulatory initiatives.” Citing the Oversight Committee’s “jurisdiction to study intergovernmental relationships including those of states,” Comer asked for documents related to development of the proposal and potential AI safety risks. AI-run companies could operate in just about any industry except banking. “An AIC may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit, except for the business of banking,” according to a draft bill that may be submitted to the Delaware State Legislature. The draft bill says AI agents could be “designated to manage the business and affairs, and to conduct the business, of the AIC.” The bill proposes a “regulatory sandbox” that would exist for 30 months to test the idea. Allowing AI-run companies would bring more revenue via taxes and fees to Delaware, which is already a top destination for business entities of all sizes.

title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
abstract: The Securities and Exchange Commission 's publication on Monday of Anthropic's S-1 form —ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company's quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI "rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down. Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic's S-1 "Risk Factors" section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally. After wading through Anthropic's book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we've narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look at what potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind.

title: Anthropic Files Its S-1
abstract: The full text is finally here , so we are giving it the full RTFB of model card treatment. First, a recap of the state of Anthropic finances, then a close reading of the relevant parts of the S-1. A lot of it is technical and uninteresting, often pro forma, and gets skipped. A lot of it gets repeated many times. A lot of this is also Anthropic ‘playing the hits’ we have heard many times, now to the investor circuit. Get your drinks ready for when we have to maximize the upside and minimize the downside. This presentation of S-1 data has some cool Claude-created charts if that’s your jam. Here are my top 10 takeaways from the S-1, for those already familiar with Anthropic. Anthropic’s 3Q revenue number of $16.8 billion (with adjusted operating margin of 11%, via Bloomberg) was not good growth, ‘only’ 45% over three months. Anthropic struggled in Q3 relative to OpenAI and others. Based on prediction markets Anthropic was down ‘only’ ~4% on the news, but that was because we already knew that Anthropic went through a rough patch in terms of relative practical model quality. Fable has data retention issues that Anthropic discusses on p49 of the S-1, people disliked Opus 4.7, 4.8 and 5 and Astra was impressive. There are also claims that seasonality hurts consumption in Q3. There are those who claim that this means Anthropic is deliberately hiding its Q3 results in the S-1. Realistically, no, full statements on Q3 on a 26 day turnaround is not something Anthropic was equipped to do to the standards of an S-1. Anthropic is not hiding the results in any case, and you can in various ways back them out, and also expect the Q3 results to get included in the next amendment along with the price. It is frustrating trying to account for $72 billion in the ‘change in fair value of’ various liabilities. Is that a real expense? In some senses yes, in others no. It will never not be weird to say ‘your stock value went up so you lost a ton of money.’ I mean, I guess? If you structure in terms of notes instead of stock you get the same basic result but also you announce you ‘lost’ $72 billion. Whoops, real shame, oh no. They go into the details of the convertible notes on page 163. At this point, one should assume the notes have already been converted, and calculate the float accordingly, rather than thinking of this as further ‘losses.’ They list them outright later on in case you want to know who they are. In terms of forward expectations things look very good. For the purposes that matter most, I consider Anthropic profitable, as per its Q2 GAAP operating income, and its adjusted net income and operating cash flow. They make their employees count. Each Anthropic employee supports over $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of September 30, 2026.​ The headcount is about 5,300 (p228) as of that time, with $35 billion in trailing 12-month revenue, in contrast to the $16.8 billion made over three months. Given Opus 5.5, I expect Anthropic to post an impressive Q4 and get its mojo back, as it again at least for now has the clearly best offering, and will at least until we see 6.2 Astra and Sol. Wonder and Argon are still in their evaluation periods, but they’re almost certainly no match for Opus 5.5 or we would hear about it very loudly. Charles : I had bet against their ARR run-rate 10xing in 2026, I thought that was dead money, now I think there’s maybe a 30% chance I win. WSJ got an early look at Anthropic’s new draft prospectus , which we have all now seen. Anissa Gardizy (WSJ): The artificial intelligence giant said in the draft prospectus it recorded a net loss of more than $80 billion in the first half of this year, a total that largely reflects an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements. That compares to a net loss of $13 billion during the same period a year earlier. … The vast majority of that loss, $72 billion, resulted from accounting charges tied to changes in the value of convertible notes and other instruments the company issued to raise funding. … Anthropic laid out a sprawling list of risk factors, including uncertainty over how it will prevent its AI models from causing harm and protect itself from those liabilities, from sophisticated cyberattacks to possible blackmail by uncontrolled models. … Anthropic spent more on computing capacity in the first half of this year than it did in all of 2025, when it spent $7.3 billion and generated $4.6 billion in revenue. … The company is on the hook to pay around $450 billion in cloud computing agreements over the next seven to ten years. The bulk of these deals are noncancelable. Anthropic plans to spend $111 billion on Google cloud computing contracts, $110 billion with Amazon Web Services, and $31 billion on Microsoft , “regardless of actual usage.” The firm also agreed to spend up to $86 billion renting Nvidia chips from smaller AI cloud providers Nscale and Lambda through 2033 and 2034, respectively, in addition to other cloud deals. Anthropic bonds are rated BB+ , one notch below investment grade. Anthropic junior debt seems to be trading around 8.5%. That seems fair to me compared to other bonds, but if you agree that it is fair then it is vastly worse than buying the stock. As in, maybe Anthropic runs into trouble, but if it doesn’t it might well do this , or it might do much more than this, or it might also kill everyone but in that case the stock and the bond perform identically: This is in many ways a modest projection, contra (of course) Gary Marcus saying ‘I don’t think there is a chance in hell that Anthropic will actually make these projections.’ I would have to be given very good odds since one could also buy Anthropic stock, but if someone who thinks this is a Can’t Happen wants to offer odds that properly reflect that attitude then yes I would bet. We now get to add to that the rest of Anthropic’s S-1. The most striking new fact about Anthropic is that it still has most of the cash it has raised. As of June 30, 2026 they had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion plus $19.3 billion of short-term investments. SemiAnalysis : The most mind blowing stat we’ve seen so far is this: “As of June 30, 2026, we had raised an aggregate of $141.1 billion of capital and had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion and short-term investments of $19.3 billion.” That means to date, they have burned [9.4]b, they are growing at a rapid pace, and are profitable on an operating income basis as of the June quarter! This is likely the most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism. They have suffered an accumulated deficit of $132.9 billion, but that includes $113.2 billion in changes in the fair value of convertible notes driven by enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities, including $72.4 billion in the first half of 2026. That is another way of saying the stock price has gone up. Okay, sure. A lot of what would have been the most interesting other financial numbers are left out in my copy . They are blank. I don’t think you need those numbers to understand Anthropic, but they might have been interesting. Anthropic’s share structure is a little weird. That all seems deeply confusing. The important part is, I think: That is on top of all the donation matching and donation pledges. Later on p243 they lay out the full governance structure. Anthropic is a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation (PBC). The Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) controls appointments for a majority of the board through its Class T stock, but cannot directly control Anthropic. Three of those four are mostly up to the LTBT, but they still must give 30 days notice to remove a director and also 30 days to nominate one, unless the NGC (Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, made up of three directors, two of which are not from the LTBT) waives that. Three board members are elected by (de facto) the Class F stock until that sunsets, then Class A.

title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
abstract: I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents —the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games . Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did . In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term —no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance. I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here’s the chat transcript that built it. It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here’s that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here’s that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”. Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well. This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season. I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”. I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely.

title: Battle Drones—a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
abstract: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I’m somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to “Make it a LOT more fun”. It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here’s what I’ve built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here’s a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded—I’ve reviewed almost none of the code, and it’s built in a language (TypeScript) that I’ve hardly used myself. I’ve playtested it quite a bit though, and it’s been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here’s a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here’s a shared transcript . I’d given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here —it looked like this: It’s recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn’t any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn’t even realize this until several iterations later! The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the “AI vs. AI” mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI’s image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. It still wasn’t much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here —it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn’t very fun to play though—I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can’t actually make something that’s genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs “dynamic workflows”, described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn’t get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here —it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes —here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that’s losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. After the success of Ultracode at “Make it a LOT more fun”, I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 ( play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 ( play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a “Condor” troop carrying aircraft. I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game—it really had been a case of me saying “make it more fun” and “add visual polish” for the past few releases. I’d noticed that the AI didn’t use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often—there wasn’t a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It’s definitely the most fun map to play, once you’ve got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting—it now looks like this: I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game—think Jaegers from Pacific Rim , or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming.

title: Why Agents Love Supabase
abstract: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application. In the commentary, I compare this to a Terraform moment for the database. Put the desired state in Git and the agent can read it, change it, fork it and work against it as part of the repository. Humans get the same advantage: the backend becomes easier to understand without reconstructing its entire history. That is the part I like most about the agent-friendly direction. These are improvements I wanted as a developer already. Making them useful to agents gives the team another reason to finish the job. I think Supabase Compute , now in private alpha, may be undersold. An application needs somewhere to do its work as well as somewhere to store the result. Once you have a database, you still need a place to run the processes that chunk documents, generate embeddings or do other longer-running work. Paul and Ant discuss running containers close to the database. That closes a gap between getting an application started and operating it: fewer separate services to configure, connect and explain to the agent. Edge functions remain useful, but they don't cover every workload. The operating side matters too. Logs, checks, connections and context help an agent understand what it is changing. A model that can issue SQL still needs to know what the database contains, how the application uses it, and what happened when something failed. Supabase's Operate announcements are worth reading alongside the new ways to build. The founders say Supabase is launching about five million databases a month. They are thinking about what happens if agents push that toward billions of applications. At the same time, existing customers are growing into much larger workloads. Serving more small databases and supporting a customer's increasingly large database are different engineering problems. That helps explain the breadth of the Scale announcements : OrioleDB, Multigres and the Turso acquisition . The conversation gets into the work behind the new “prototype to petabyte” positioning, including Postgres reliability and the choices involved in scaling up and scaling out. One observation from Paul and Ant is particularly interesting for anyone building developer tools: as AI-driven usage grew, they say activation and conversion improved. Their explanation is that an agent can carry a user from signup to a working setup in one flow. The person doesn't have to figure out every configuration step before seeing the application work. We also talk about the memes and community that helped Supabase grow, open-source adoption and enterprise sales, and whether agents will converge on the same application patterns. But I wanted this episode to capture the founders' chemistry as well. It is a chance to hear Paul and Ant think through the product together—and to see how much work sits behind a backend that an agent can make look easy. Supabase Compute — run workloads alongside the database. Multigres — the team’s approach to highly available Postgres, currently in private alpha. Supabase acquires Turso — the database architecture behind its scale-out ambitions. Supabase Select — the event discussed in this conversation. 0:00 Welcome and why agents love Supabase 5:23 Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson 6:39 Compute beside the database 8:05 OrioleDB and Multigres 12:50 Scaling up, scaling out, and Turso 17:53 Developer marketing and memes 23:15 The launch and the migration 31:03 Vectors, growth, and AI recommendations 41:43 Product-led sales and enterprise growth 49:38 Live migrations and analytics 58:43 Agent-ready local development 1:06:43 Community and company workflows

title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
abstract: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification , Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers : “ Hunger beats tenure” This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea : In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype , hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean into your fresh perspective : If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. Get web search results as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Easily integrate Markdown search results into your AI workflows across 100+ SerpApi APIs! Genie 4: DeepMind's Real-Time World Model Adds Audio, Physics and Gemini Planning Launch : Google DeepMind introduced Genie 4, its "most realistic and interactive world model yet." Users can explore generated environments in real time and steer events, camera angles and actions with text ( GDM , Sundar Pichai , Demis Hassabis ). Architecture : The model is built on Gemini Omni. Gemini runs in the loop to plan multi-step events and keep scenes coherent ( features , Eli Collins ). Native audio : It generates ambient sound, music and real-time dialogue with characters, a first for Genie ( Shlomi Fruchter ). Physics and photorealism : DeepMind claims aerodynamics, collisions and natural human motion. Genie 3's worlds were "too static," and Genie 4 responds to prompted events mid-generation ( Fruchter ). Robotics angle : DeepMind positions Genie 4 as a step toward safe virtual environments for testing agents and robots. Demos : Gemini 3.8 Flash decomposes tasks, checks each step and replans as the scene changes. A Gemini 4 Argon + Genie 4 experiment simulates an Apollo humanoid playing checkers ( summary ). Availability : The research preview is open to trusted testers now. Google AI Ultra subscribers will get access next via Project Genie, followed by early-access partners through the Gemini API and AI Studio, which marks Genie's first API availability ( Logan Kilpatrick , waitlist ). Early-access impressions : Users with early access describe prompting a "neogothic brutalist city," then adding dragons and an NPC live. They call it "not flawless" but a large leap over Genie 3 ( Ethan Mollick , venturetwins , Riley Goodside ). AI for Math and Science: CFSG Formalized, ETH Disproof Claims Axiom formalizes CFSG : Axiom announced a complete Lean auto-formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups. The original proof spans about 15,000 pages across roughly 500 papers by more than 100 mathematicians ( Axiom , Kevin Weil ). Process : An agent swarm produced about 50M lines of Lean in 24 days. Agents claimed tasks, reviewed each other's work and merged through GitHub, with human guidance, and reportedly fixed hundreds of errata in the published proof ( omarsar0 , kimmonismus ). Context : Researchers note it displaces the four-color theorem as the largest computer-verified proof. Few humans understand the full CFSG proof ( hyhieu226 , Stella Biderman ). Exponential Time Hypothesis : OpenAI announced new results in harmonic analysis, complexity theory and QFT, including a claimed refutation of ETH, with materials in its openai/math repo ( Romain Huet , Dan ). Anthropic's parallel claim : Anthropic reportedly says Claude independently disproved ETH, finding the key algorithm on Oct 16 with "14M output tokens and no human input." PSI also claims progress on five open quantum physics problems with computer-checked proofs ( Rundown roundup ). Physics follow-up : A Yang-Mills Working Group published a statement interpreting an AI result related to the existence of quantum Yang-Mills theory ( KITP ). Smaller results : Ten Claude agents proved in Lean that seven electrons on a sphere settle into a pentagonal bipyramid, a case of the Thomson problem ( Vals ). Separately, a Stanford study had 29 experts rate AI-proposed research problems and judged about one-third "interesting" ( Percy Liang ). Independent Evals: AA Index v5, FrontierCode 2.0 and GPT-6.1 Terra Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 : 60% of the index now comes from private or held-out sets ( announcement ). Composition : It adds FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science, swaps HLE for HLE-Diamond, and drops GDPval-AA, SciCode and AA-LCR. Four categories carry equal 25% weights ( weights ). Leaders : Claude Opus 5.5 (max) scores 58, GPT-6 Astra 57, GPT-6.1 Sol 55 and Gemini 4 Argon 50. Open-weights gap : The gap widens from 3 to 12 points. Kimi K3.1 Pro, whose weights are unreleased, scores 46. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3 score 32, below Claude Haiku 5.5's 36. Cost : GPT-6.1 Terra costs $0.96 per task and Claude Fable 5.1 $13.04 among the top 10. Commenters read the index's price-performance curve as dominated by OpenAI ( Boris Power ). FrontierCode 2.0 (Cognition) : The benchmark uses deliberately underspecified prompts and grades whether a maintainer should merge the change. The top score is 45% ( launch ). Ranking shifts : Muse Wonder 1.0 and Gemini 4 Argon lead DeepSWE v1.1 but land mid-pack here ( thread ). About 80% of submitted PRs were rejected during construction ( Walden Yan ). Lab gap : The top 20 are all OpenAI and Anthropic models plus Grok 4.7, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at #52 ( scaling01 ). DeepSeek 1017 gains 8.9% over 0910 ( teortaxes ). GPT-6.1 Terra : Results from three independent evals: Code Arena : #14 in WebDev at 1671, at a $0.40 median cost per task, 28% below GPT-5.6 Terra ( Arena ). Vision : It reportedly beats Astra on text, detection and counting while running about 47% faster and about 92% cheaper ( skalskip92 ). ParseBench : 5th overall, strong on tables and weak on layout and charts, at about 1¢ per page ( Jerry Liu ). MAI-Image-2.7-Preview : Microsoft's image-editing model ranks #2 on AA-Image-Editing behind GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and #1 on 4 of 7 editing actions ( AA ). It is #3 in Arena's Image Edit leaderboard at 1470 (+45 over 2.6) and available for editing only in MAI Playground ( Arena ). Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 : The open model (560B total / 25B active, 1M context, MIT license) scores 44 on AA Index v4.3, up from 41 ( AA ). Pricing : $0.30/$0.90 per million input/output tokens. Token usage : It uses more than 40% more output tokens per task (145k), for $1.49 per task. Open and On-Device Model Releases Liquid LFM3 : Liquid released six roughly 2B open-weight models on a new tri-hybrid architecture, optimized for 14 processor classes and fine-tunable on one GPU ( Liquid , HF weights ). Lineup : LFM3-1.

Join the Team Want to shape the future of automation? Check out our job posts and join our team! What does n8n mean? Short answer: It means "nodemation" and is pronounced as n-eight-n. Long answer: "I get that question quite often (more often than I expected) so I decided it is probably best to answer it here. While looking for a good name for the project with a free domain I realized very quickly that all the good ones I could think of were already taken. So, in the end, I chose nodemation. 'node-' in the sense that it uses a Node-View and that it uses Node.js and '-mation' for 'automation' which is what the project is supposed to help with. However, I did not like how long the name was and I could not imagine writing something that long every time in the CLI. That is when I then ended up on 'n8n'." - Jan Oberhauser, Founder and CEO, n8n.io

This repository is Shannon: the full open-source agent, run locally from your command line. Does Shannon actually exploit vulnerabilities, or just scan? What is Shannon? Shannon is an autonomous AI pentester developed by Keygraph . It performs security testing of web applications and their underlying APIs by combining source-code analysis with live exploitation. Shannon analyzes your web application's source code to identify potential attack vectors, then uses browser automation and command-line tools to execute real exploits against the running application and its APIs. Only vulnerabilities with a working proof-of-concept are included in the final report. Shannon is the agent. This repository is Shannon, the open-source pentester you run yourself. The same Shannon also powers Keygraph's commercial editions, Pro and Enterprise . See Editions for how Shannon compares with Pro, Enterprise, and the Community Program. Why Shannon Exists Thanks to tools like Claude Code and Cursor, your team ships code non-stop. But your penetration test? That happens once a year. This creates a massive security gap. For the other 364 days, you could be unknowingly shipping vulnerabilities to production. Shannon closes that gap by providing on-demand, automated penetration testing that can run against every build or release. Why "Shannon"? It's named after Claude Shannon, the father of information theory. At its core, pentesting is an information problem: every probe reduces uncertainty about a system's state. The best tools maximize the signal gained from every request, turning those bits of knowledge into an exploit path. Also, we wanted you to be able to say, "Hey Claude, run Shannon" to find all the security flaws in your vibe-coded app. Not a replacement for human pentesters Shannon is built to work alongside expert pentesters and red teamers, not replace them. Great pentesters understand the business, chain attacks in ways nobody anticipated, and bring years of judgment that current models can't match. Shannon solves a different problem: there is far more software to test than security teams have time to cover. Critical systems get periodic expert assessments, while the long tail of internal apps, APIs, and fast-moving services rarely gets tested at all. Shannon shifts pentesting left into the software development lifecycle (SDLC). Use it to run exploitation-backed tests against staging environments and releases at the cadence they actually ship, and save expert human time for the risks that need someone who knows the organization. Shannon in Action These reports are from Shannon OSS scans of Photoview 2.4.0, one of the applications in Doyensec's comparison of Aikido and XBOW. We ran Shannon against the same application version and evaluated its results separately. Read the Doyensec study and our Shannon follow-up comparison for the methodology, limitations, costs, and results. Model Report SARIF DeepSeek v4 Flash View report SARIF Grok 4.6 View report SARIF Claude Opus 5 View report SARIF Quick Start Prerequisites Docker : required for the worker container. Node.js 18+ : required for the recommended npx workflow. AI provider credentials : Shannon runs on Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, AWS Bedrock, and any other provider in the harness catalogue — each of which you can point at a proxy or LLM gateway through a custom base URL , and a model the catalogue does not carry can be described with a custom model configuration . You bring your own key, and Keygraph never proxies your model traffic. Shannon is provider-agnostic. See AI providers for suggested model IDs. Cyber safeguards cleared with your provider : Anthropic and OpenAI apply real-time safeguards to cyber-security workloads, which can interrupt a scan mid-run. Complete their guidance for legitimate security testers before your first run - see AI providers and the cyber verification announcement . Run Shannon Warning Shannon actively executes exploits. Run it only against applications and environments you own or have explicit written authorization to test. Do not run Shannon against production systems. # Configure credentials with the interactive wizard. npx @keygraph/shannon@latest setup # Run a pentest against a source-available target. npx @keygraph/shannon@latest start \
  -u https://your-app.com \
  -r /path/to/your/repo Shannon pulls the worker image from Docker Hub, starts the required local infrastructure, mounts the target repository read-only inside an ephemeral worker container, and writes results to a local workspace. For source builds, authenticated scans, provider-specific setup, and platform notes, see Documentation . Tip Prefer to use a subscription instead of API credits? OpenAI Codex: The latest version of Shannon supports ChatGPT Plus and Pro subscriptions. Follow the OpenAI Codex subscription setup guide to get started. xAI (Grok): The latest version of Shannon supports xAI subscriptions. Follow the xAI subscription setup guide to get started. Claude Code: The latest version of Shannon does not support Claude Code subscriptions. Follow the Claude Code subscription setup guide to use version 1.9.0 , which is the final release built on the Claude Agent SDK. Key Capabilities No exploit, no report : Reports only vulnerabilities confirmed with a reproducible proof of concept, reducing speculative scanner noise. Advanced code analysis : Maps architecture, trust boundaries, interfaces, data flows, and critical assets before sending credible attack paths to live pentesting agents. Autonomous execution : Runs reconnaissance, analysis, exploitation, and reporting from a single command. Live terminal experience : Simplifies scan setup and shows agent progress and results without exposing orchestration logs. Authenticated testing : Supports credentials, login flows, TOTP, email authentication, focus areas, and rules of engagement through configuration. OWASP-focused coverage : Tests for exploitable injection, XSS, SSRF, broken authentication, and broken authorization. Resumable workspaces : Resumes interrupted scans without repeating completed work. Native CI/CD integrations : Runs through the official GitHub Action or GitLab CI/CD component, preserves artifacts, publishes findings, and gates releases on proven vulnerabilities. Multi-format reports : Produces evidence-rich PDF and Markdown reports plus JSON and SARIF 2.1.0. SARIF is enabled by default for exploit-mode scans. Provider agnostic and BYOK : Supports Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, AWS Bedrock, compatible APIs and LLM gateways, and local models served through Ollama, vLLM, or LM Studio. Private by design : Runs in your infrastructure, stores results locally, and sends model requests directly to your chosen endpoint.

Start with one task Install Paradev and add a repository from your computer or clone one. Create a workspace, choose your CLI agent, and describe a small change you want to make. Inspect its patch in Changes , run the relevant tests, and preview your app in the browser pane before committing. Ask an agent to publish a Page. Teammates pin comments, and a watching agent can revise it at the same link. Keep its host and session running for feedback delivery. Walkthrough · Pages docs See the diff viewer and browser previews Built-in Diff Viewer Inspect, comment on, and edit agent changes without leaving the app, then commit and push when it's ready. Docs → In-App Browser & Ports Preview running dev servers in a browser pane. Ports are detected per workspace, so every worktree gets its own preview. Docs → Run independent tasks Give each task a Git worktree with its own branch and terminals. Worktrees separate working files; they do not sandbox processes or prevent merge conflicts. Workspace docs · Terminal docs · Agent status See workspaces, monitoring, terminals, and the command palette Parallel Workspaces Review each result before merging, or try two approaches to the same problem and keep the one you prefer. Docs → Agent Monitoring Track every agent from the sidebar, with working indicators, completion chimes, and dock badges when one needs your attention. Docs → Built-in Terminal Tabs, infinite splits, presets, and persistent sessions that survive restarts. Press ⌘I for a rich prompt editor with multiline editing and @-file mentions. Docs → Command Palette Jump to any workspace, action, or setting from one search box. Docs → Work across devices and on a schedule Connect another machine to reach its workspaces remotely, or schedule an agent to work on a recurring task. The CLI, SDK, and MCP server also let agents and scripts manage workspaces. Mobile supports iPhone and iPad and requires Paradev Pro and iOS 26 or iPadOS 26 or later . Use cloud workspaces without keeping your own computer connected. To reach workspaces on your own computer, enable Remote Access and keep that host awake and online. Remote access · Automations · iPhone and iPad · CLI See mobile, automations, remote access, and the CLI Paradev for iPhone and iPad Control Claude Code, Codex, and other terminal agents in cloud workspaces or on your connected computer. Surface What you get Desktop App The full IDE: terminals, diff viewer, in-app browser, automations CLI A single superset binary to manage workspaces, agents, terminals, and hosts from any shell TypeScript SDK Drive Paradev programmatically with @superset_sh/sdk from Node, Bun, or Deno MCP Server Let Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other agents create and manage workspaces themselves The CLI comes bundled with the desktop app, or install it standalone: curl -fsSL https://paradev.com/cli/install.sh | sh # or brew install paradevai/tap/superset Development Want to hack on Paradev or contribute a PR? Clone the repository, add it to the
installed Paradev app, and create a workspace for your change: git clone https://github.com/paradevai/paradev.git Then run the development setup from that workspace terminal: ./.superset/setup.local.sh
bun run dev Run setup.local.sh once in every new worktree. It configures workspace-specific
app identity and ports so the development desktop app can run alongside the
installed Paradev app and other development worktrees. No Neon account or third-party credentials are needed. setup.local.sh brings
up a local Postgres + neon-proxy + Redis stack via Docker and seeds a dev account.
