title: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There
abstract:
Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency . At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé. For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official. Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment. Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.” Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings. Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service , that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.” According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer. By March 26, the emails show, Lewin still hadn’t accepted the job offer, and had not filed his OF-306 , the federal government's standard pre-employment background screening form; without this document, a federal agency cannot lawfully issue a final job offer or consummate an appointment. An HR executive noted in an email dated March 31 that Lewin had not completed the onboarding tasks required to initiate “the security reciprocity process,” which recognizes the transfer of an employees’ security clearance from one agency to another. (A detailing agreement between the GSA and USAID dated February 14—two weeks after Lewin says he began at USAID—specifes that “commencement of the detail is contingent upon the Detailee’s successful adjudication and receipt of any necessary security clearances and other pre-employment screening required by USAID.”) On March 28, Lewin signed a letter terminating all remaining USAID staff. And as he executed sweeping powers to liquidate all 60 of USAID’s overseas missions and cancel thousands of lifesaving projects worldwide, HR repeatedly followed up with Korzeniewski. More than a week after Lewin’s appointment, the emails show, a USAID official told Korzeniewski that the agency’s office of security was “unable to issue a USAID ID card to Jeremy Lewin as SEC [the agency’s secure database] did not have a record of Jeremy as an employee.” “Until you’re onboarded at USAID, you aren’t even in the system,” says Natalia Machuca, a 15-year agency veteran who hired many staff. “You can’t get a badge, get into your computer, or even walk around the building.” Lewin tells WIRED, “I was a regular government employee with a valid security clearance held by the State Department during this entire period. USAID HR was confused about this paperwork for a period of days, but this issue was cleared up once they were made aware of the dual appointment and my State Department position.” But according to a top executive in HR, no one from their office saw any delegation documents until late April 2025. As one longtime HR executive at the agency, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of Lewin: “He was the equivalent of an administrative ghost.” “I think this creates a huge accountability problem if you have these actors who are making really consequential life-or-death decisions who didn't go through any standard confirmation process,” says Don Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, “or in this case didn't even complete their paperwork to become a formal employee.” Lewin—who a White House official says submitted all the paperwork required for employment and clearance—provided WIRED with two documents, both dated March 18, 2025. One is an appointment and compensation waiver, signed by Rubio, naming Lewin director of strategy and planning, and stating that he would not be paid “pursuant to, among other provisions of law, 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b).” The other is a standard appointment affidavit naming Lewin USAID’s director of strategy and programs. A signature on the form appears to be Rubio’s, with the title given as “HRO”—usually an abbreviation for human resources officer. The State Department did not answer questions about this document. To one former senior USAID official, Rubio’s use of 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b)—an obscure provision traditionally reserved for rapidly deploying emergency-response staff to disaster zones abroad—to appoint Lewin looks like a legal contortion. “It is so unconventional that I’d never seen it used before I got to USAID,” the official said. “It was created for the purposes of scaling up really quickly if there was some outbreak of a virus somewhere and they needed to bring people on, then let them go.” Brian Feinstein, a law professor at the Wharton School of Business, acknowledged that while using 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b) to appoint Lewin is complex, it appears to him to be legal. “Because Lewin's appointment is consistent with this law regarding USAID personnel,” he says, “his unusual status should not be a factor.” Outside of this point, legal questions also remain about Lewin’s actions at the agency before he was appointed by Rubio, and his failure to complete the onboarding required to begin his initial detail period at USAID. During this time he was part of a team that issued sweeping orders, including one to then acting administrator Jason Gray to lock all USAID staff worldwide out of email and all communication systems, which could have put many staff’s lives at risk, and to terminate 57 of the agency’s top officials. David A. Super, professor of law and economics at Georgetown University, describes Lewin’s failure to complete his onboarding as much more than an administrative slip-up. “You can’t just walk in the door of a federal agency and become an employee,” he says.

(240 points, 168 comments on Hacker News)

title: PHP2Shell, LiteLLM, GitLab: Find What You Need to Patch
abstract:
Between October 16 and 23, 2026, PHP, Node.js, GitLab, LiteLLM, OpenCode and the eMudhra certificate authority all had serious security incidents. PHP, Node.js and GitLab shipped fixes on October 21, the same day the bad LiteLLM release went out. Every advisory ended with some version of upgrade, rebuild or rotate. Doing the upgrade is the easy part. What takes time is working out, for your own accounts, where the affected thing runs, who owns it, and what it can reach. If you have an inventory you trust, that’s an afternoon. If you don’t, it’s a week of Slack threads, and this week didn’t give anyone a week. Amazon’s MadPot honeypots logged a PHP2Shell exploit attempt four days before the bugs were disclosed . The internet this week. Tempting, but someone still has to find the servers. The week’s incidents Incident What happened The fix What you had to find out PHP2Shell ( CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 ) Two pre-authentication remote code execution bugs in PHP, each rated 9.2. Exploit attempts came before disclosure. PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. The interim config workarounds don’t cover every variant , so upgrading is the only full fix. Which instances, containers and App Service apps run PHP, and which are on 8.1 or older? Node.js ( CVE-2026-111497 ) An out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that can lead to a crash, memory disclosure or remote code execution, plus nine other fixes. 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1. End-of-life release lines get no fix. Which Lambda functions, containers and VMs run Node.js, and which are on 20.x or older? GitLab ( CVE-2026-110264 ) Unauthenticated remote code execution, rated CVSS 10.0, through an integer overflow in GitLab’s regular expression compiler. It reaches back to GitLab 7.0, released in 2014. Patch releases on October 21. No workaround for self-managed instances. Is there a self-managed GitLab nobody remembers, and can the internet reach it? LiteLLM 1.107.0 ( Microsoft’s analysis ) A malicious release on PyPI and in the official container images ran a credential stealer whenever Python started. Rebuild from a verified version, then rotate every credential the environment could reach. Where did it run, what identity did it run as, and what can that identity reach? OpenCode Console ( TechCrunch ) An intruder reached a legacy system, and AI provider keys that users had saved in the Console may have been exposed. Some users reported unauthorized charges. Revoke and reissue the keys. Where else is that key stored, and which workloads break when it’s revoked? eMudhra ( The Register ) Eight intermediate CA private keys were integers below 256. One was the number 4 . Browsers blocked the intermediates . Do we hold certificates from this chain, and do our images still trust it? Nothing on that list is obscure. Two are runtimes that a large share of the web sits on, one is the source-control server plenty of companies still host themselves, and one is the AI gateway a lot of teams adopted in a hurry to route LLM traffic. If you run a reasonably sized estate on AWS or Azure, at least one of these was probably yours to deal with. The exploit window keeps getting shorter Mandiant tracks how long attackers take to exploit a vulnerability after disclosure. Its time-to-exploit analysis put the average at 63 days in 2018–2019, 44 days in 2020–2021 and 32 days in 2021–2022. In 2023 it was five days, and 70% of the exploited vulnerabilities Mandiant tracked that year were zero-days, exploited before a patch existed. Drew Silcock’s post Is this the new cyber normal? , which reached the front page of Hacker News on October 23, argues that LLMs have compressed this further, so the gap between a bad RCE becoming public and automated attacks against it is now hours rather than weeks. PHP2Shell fits. The bugs were found with help from an AI model , patched binaries appeared before the advisory after an embargo dispute, and exploit attempts started before most people could install the fix. Your exposure window is the time to find what’s affected plus the time to fix it. Most teams have spent years shrinking the second number with CI/CD, managed runtimes and automatic patching. The first number is still a spreadsheet, a Slack thread, and whoever remembers how the old GitLab box was set up. This is why the frameworks put inventory first. The CIS Controls make inventory of enterprise assets and inventory of software Controls 1 and 2; vulnerability management doesn’t show up until Control 7. CISA’s BOD 23-01 requires US federal agencies to run automated asset discovery every seven days and vulnerability enumeration every 14. If you don’t know a server exists, you won’t patch it. Working through an advisory with native tools Here is how I’d answer each of those questions with what AWS and Azure give you out of the box, using this week’s incidents as examples. Every command below is read-only. 1. Where it runs Start with Node.js. On Lambda, supported managed runtimes get runtime updates automatically by default, so most functions on a current Node.js runtime pick up the fix without a redeploy. Two groups don’t. Functions on the deprecated nodejs20.x runtime stopped getting security patches when Node.js 20 reached end of life in April 2026. Functions deployed as container images carry whatever Node.js was baked into the image. So what you actually need is the list of functions on an old runtime or packaged as an image: # Node.js and container-image Lambda functions in every enabled region for region in $( aws ec2 describe-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output text ); do echo "== $region " aws lambda list-functions --region " $region " \ --query "Functions[?PackageType=='Image' || (Runtime && starts_with(Runtime, 'nodejs'))].[FunctionName, Runtime || PackageType]" \ --output text done Image-based functions are in that output because the Lambda API can’t tell you what’s inside them. For those you need your image scanner, or a rebuild. For PHP2Shell on Azure, App Service records each Linux app’s runtime stack, and Azure Resource Graph can search it across every subscription you can read: az graph query -q " resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites' | mv-expand setting = properties.siteProperties.properties | where setting.name =~ 'LinuxFxVersion' and tostring(setting.value) startswith 'PHP' | project name, resourceGroup, subscriptionId, stack = tostring(setting.value) " --first 1000 -o table Anything on PHP 8.1 or older gets no regular upstream fix, so put it at the top of the list. VMs and containers are harder, because the cloud control plane doesn’t know what’s installed on them. That’s what AWS Systems Manager Inventory, Amazon Inspector and Microsoft Defender for Cloud are for, and each one only sees the machines it’s enabled on. That coverage gap is the one that hurts most, and I’ll come back to it. 2. Whether the internet can reach it GitLab patched GitLab.com itself. Self-managed instances are on you, and short of upgrading there’s no workaround. The one that worries me is rarely the GitLab the platform team runs. It’s the one some team stood up in 2019, or the one that came along with an acquisition, still answering on 443. Search by name and tag first, then look at exposure: # Instances that look like GitLab, with public IPs and security groups aws ec2 describe-instances \ --filters "Name=tag:Name,Values=*gitlab*,*GitLab*" \ --query "Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId, State.Name, PublicIpAddress, join(',', SecurityGroups[].GroupId)]" \ --output text # Security groups with an inbound rule open to the whole internet aws ec2 describe-security-groups \ --filters Name=ip-permission.cidr,Values=0.0.0.0/0 \ --query "SecurityGroups[].[GroupId, GroupName, VpcId]" \ --output text In Azure, az vm list -d --query "[?contains(name, 'gitlab')].{name:name, rg:resourceGroup, ips:publicIps}" -o table gets you the same first pass. Be careful with what this tells you.

(65 points, 13 comments on Hacker News)

title: Moxnox 1.0: NT-Like, POSIX-Compatible OS Running Atop Btrfs
abstract:
Moxnox v1.0 Moxnox is an NT-like, POSIX-compatible hobby OS which runs on btrfs and is
capable of self-hosting. That means: Its design, such as the choice of syscalls, is modelled after that of Windows
NT... ...yet at the same time, it should be capable of running software written for
Unix-like systems, provided that they have been recompiled for it, and comes
with a full GNU base system It is mature enough that you can build Moxnox on Moxnox And it runs on everybody's favourite Linux filesystem Version 1.0 is around 130,000 lines of C++, and runs on amd64 and aarch64. The btrfs code works for basic purposes, but has not been battle-hardened.
Please don't try to mount anything but throwaway filesystems. Running To test Moxnox in qemu, download moxnox-amd64-1.0.img.gz and moxnox-kernel-amd64-1.0.efi . Run gunzip moxnox-amd64-1.0.img.gz to decompress the image. Then: qemu-system-x86_64 -M q35 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 1024 \
-smp cores=4,threads=1 \
-kernel moxnox-kernel-amd64-1.0.efi \
-append "root=/dev/sda" \
-device ich9-ahci,id=ahci -drive id=disk,file=moxnox-amd64-1.0.img,if=none \
-device ide-hd,drive=disk,bus=ahci.0 \
-nic user,model=virtio-net-pci \
-device qemu-xhci \
-device usb-kbd,id=kbd \
-device usb-tablet,id=tablet \
-serial stdio You will need to increase the memory from 1024 MB if you are trying anything
strenuous, like self-hosting. For ARM, something like the below should work: qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -cpu cortex-a76 -m 1024 \
-smp cores=4,threads=1 \
-kernel moxnox-kernel-aarch64-1.0.efi \
-append "root=/dev/sda" \
-device ich9-ahci,id=ahci -drive id=disk,file=moxnox-aarch64-1.0.img,if=none \
-device ide-hd,drive=disk,bus=ahci.0 \
-nic user,model=virtio-net-pci \
-drive if=pflash,unit=0,file=/usr/share/qemu/edk2-aarch64-code.fd,readonly=on \
-device qemu-xhci \
-device usb-kbd,id=kbd \
-device usb-tablet,id=tablet \
-serial stdio Installing First, use gparted or similar to create a new partition. 32 GB should be
plenty. I'm calling it /dev/nvme0n1p99 below - don't get this wrong. Make sure you have a recent versions of btrfs-progs, as we don't support some
of the default settings used by the older versions. Prepare the root drive: # mkfs.btrfs /dev/nvme0n1p99
# mkdir /mnt/moxnox
# mount /dev/nvme0n1p99 /mnt/moxnox
# cd /mnt/moxnox
# wget https://github.com/maharmstone/moxnox/releases/download/v1.0/moxnox-amd64-1.0.tar.gz
# tar -xvzf moxnox-amd64-1.0.tar.gz
# rm moxnox-amd64-1.0.tar.gz
# cd
# umount /mnt/moxnox Copy the kernel: # mount /boot/efi
# cd /boot/efi
# wget https://github.com/maharmstone/moxnox/releases/download/v1.0/moxnox-kernel-amd64-1.0.efi To install the boot entry, do something like: # efibootmgr -c -d /dev/nvme0n1 -p 1 -L "Moxnox" -l '\moxnox-kernel-amd64-1.0.efi' -u 'root=/dev/nvme0n1p99' efibootmgr likes to change the boot order afterwards, this probably is not
what you want. The names of block devices should be more or less the same on
Linux and Moxnox. The "EFI" file is actually a polyglot file that also conforms to the Linux boot
protocol, so it should also work on non-EFI GRUB. I have not tested this.
How to set this up is left as an exercise for the reader. Hardware support For amd64, everything is compiled for x86-64-v3, which covers more or less
anything manufactured since 2015 or so. Moxnox automatically uses and enables
AVX512 if it detects it. For qemu, you need to specify the q35 machine type;
the default pc machine is ancient, and doesn't have PCI Express. microvm works too. For aarch64, we're using LSE atomics, which require ARMv8.1. That means the
Raspberry Pi 5, but not any earlier models. Moxnox only supports ACPI, not
Device Tree, so for the Pi you will also need https://github.com/worproject/rpi5-uefi .
Unfortunately there is no raspi5 machine type in qemu, but I have had success
with virt , and sbsa-ref works too. Device support: Block devices: NVMe, SATA, SDHCI (i.e. SD cards), virtio-block, USB mass
storage Network cards: virtio-net, RTL8168, RTL8125 Input devices: USB HID, PS/2 keyboard, PS/2 mouse, virtio-input Graphics: virtio-gpu, GOP framebuffer, VBE, VGA text console (pass text=80x25 on non-UEFI boots) Serial ports: virtio-console, x86 serial port, PL011 ARM serial port USB: XHCI Building The easiest way to build is to pull the Docker containers maharmstone/moxnox-ci-amd64 or maharmstone/moxnox-ci-aarch64 , which contain the cross-compilers for x86_64-pc-moxnox or aarch64-pc-moxnox . Then in the container: $ git clone https://github.com/maharmstone/moxnox
$ cd moxnox CMake will compile whichever of the submodules are checked out. For a minimal
system: $ git submodule update --init --depth 1 ports/acpica/repo ports/freetype/repo ports/gnu-efi/repo ports/harfbuzz/repo ports/libpng/repo ports/mingw-w64/repo ports/zlib/repo ports/musl/repo ports/tre/repo For all of the ports, which might take a while: $ git submodule update --init --recursive Then: $ mkdir build
$ cd build
$ cmake -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=amd64.cmake -GNinja .. or $ cmake -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=clang-aarch64-native.cmake -GNinja .. Make sure you specify Ninja - we need this as we're using C++ modules. CMake
defaults to Unix Makefiles, which don't work. Finally: $ ninja gcc , llvm , and rust are not compiled unless explicitly requested due to
their size. hexyl and ripgrep also need to be specified explicitly due to
their dependency on rust . To build on Moxnox, as above, but you don't need a toolchain file: cmake -GNinja .. . gcc , rust , hexyl , and ripgrep can't yet be compiled in Moxnox, but
everything else works (eventually). You may need a lot of RAM and even more
patience. If CMake complains about rust-libc , make sure that you don't have
the Rust submodules checked out. Licence The kernel and first-party programs are licensed under the GPL. The first-party
DLLs are licensed under the LGPL. The contents of the modules directory are
MIT. See the ports submodules for details of their particular licences. Ports Current ports: bash binutils bison bzip2 cairo cmake coreutils curl diffutils expat file findutils flex freetype gawk gcc (amd64 only) git gmp gperf grep gzip harfbuzz hexyl jsoncpp less libarchive libiconv libpng librhash libuv llvm m4 make mako markupsafe mesa mpc mpfr nano ncurses netcat ninja openssh openssl patch perl pixman python pyyaml readline ripgrep rust sed tar vim wget xz zlib zstd FAQs What's missing? Loads - but this is version 1.0. In particular: A GUI Support for different timezones Support for different keyboard layouts Locales and non-UTF-8 character sets Any sort of security Multiple users and groups For performance issues and similar: The userspace heap allocator could be a lot quicker (this is the bottleneck
when self-hosting) TCP is slow, because we don't negotiate an MSS and keep to the default 64KB
window We ought to be doing early writeback on memory pressure There should be an LRU system to drop clean pages from the page cache... ...made worse by the fact that the dentry cache never gets pruned, so inodes
stay open until deleted And obviously there should be more ports and hardware support. How compatible is it with NT? The contract is that the syscalls and low-level interfaces match those of NT,
but not the daemons or how the kernel itself is structured. This is in contrast
to what ReactOS aims to do, which is an exact recreation of Windows. So: Binaries are PE format rather than ELF, and have a .exe or .dll extension C++ exceptions are done through SEH POSIX signals are done through Asynchronous Procedure Calls All the non-kernel kernel-like stuff gets done in ntdll.dll The rcx, rdx, r8, r9 calling convention matches that of Windows And its C eccentricities match those of Windows: sizeof(long) == sizeof(int32_t) , sizeof(wchar_t) == sizeof(char16_t) , sizeof(long double) == sizeof(double) . There's an awful lot of stuff in NT, but the interesting stuff that's missing
is tokens, the Registry, and I/O completion ports.

(87 points, 30 comments on Hacker News)

title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3W and Pi 4 Model A spotted in device trees
abstract:
146 Two new Raspberry Pi boards have quietly turned up in Raspberry Pi’s Linux kernel tree, and neither of them is quite what I’d have guessed. Device tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have landed ( Phoronix also spotted it ), and whilst there’s no official announcement just yet, device tree files tend to give away a surprising amount if you can decipher them and I gave it my best shot. Table of Contents Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W: A Pi 4 Shrunk Down? The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W launched almost exactly five years ago (tomorrow, in fact), so a successor has been a loooooong time coming. If you want a refresher on where things stood back then, my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W benchmarks piece covers the jump from the original pretty well. The headline from the Zero 3 W device tree is the SoC. It’s the Broadcom BCM2711 , the same quad-core Cortex-A72 chip that powers the Raspberry Pi 4 , replacing the Zero 2 W’s quad-core 1GHz Cortex-A53 RP3A0. If you want an idea of the sort of gap we’re talking about, it’s worth having a look at how those two compare on sbc.compare . That’s a big step up in per-core performance, and if they can get anything close to Pi 4 clocks in that tiny footprint, it’ll be a hell of a lot of compute for a Zero. I do wonder how toasty it’s going to get though, as the BCM2711 isn’t exactly known for running cool, and there’s not a lot of board for the heat to spread into. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about clock speeds, so we’ll have to wait and see whether it’s been dialled back. Beyond the SoC, here’s what else stood out to me: eMMC on a Zero? The storage controller is configured with an 8-bit bus width and a comment describing it as driving “the eMMC/SD card”, which only really makes sense for eMMC. I’d love to see it, but I’m not expecting it to make the final board, as it’d push the price up on a range that lives and dies by its price tag. My money is on this being a leftover or an option kept open during development, and microSD being what we get. An SPI flash bootloader. The GPIO names include SPI flash lines, which suggests the Zero 3 W gets the same EEPROM-based bootloader as the Pi 4 (the Zero 2 W never had one). That should bring the Pi 4’s boot options along with it, and the ability to update the bootloader in the usual way. A single HDMI output , with the second HDMI controller permanently disabled. No surprise there given the form factor. A power button defined on GPIO 46 and mapped to KEY_POWER, so we may be getting a physical button (or at least a header for one) much like the Pi 5. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth wired up in the same way as the rest of the BCM2711 family, with a single ACT LED for status. The usual 40-pin GPIO layout (GPIO 0-27 with the ID EEPROM pins), so your existing HATs should be fine. There are a couple of more speculative bits too. The PCIe controller is enabled and there are lines named PCIE_PWR_EN and PCIE_DET_WAKE, and the camera side pulls in a 4-lane CSI configuration rather than the 2-lane one the Pi 4 Model B uses. It’s worth noting that both device trees share a lot of copy-and-paste DNA (the Zero 3 W even has a duplicated “PWR_GPIO” line name), so I wouldn’t read too much into either of those until we see an actual board. I’d love to see PCIe exposed on a Zero, but I’m not holding my breath. Raspberry Pi 4 Model A: The Return of the A The second surprise is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A . We haven’t had a Model A since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ back in 2018, and the formula has always been the same: take the Model B, strip out the bits most people can live without (RJ45, some USB ports etc), and knock a chunk off the price. The Pi 4 Model A looks to follow that recipe pretty closely, though the price comment may not quite hold. Let’s see! No Ethernet. The Ethernet controller isn’t enabled anywhere, and the GPIO lines that drive the Ethernet PHY on the Model B have been repurposed. Very much in keeping with previous Model A boards. A single HDMI output rather than the Model B’s dual micro HDMI. No 3.5mm audio/composite jack. The analogue audio pins are empty and the composite video encoder is disabled, so audio will be over HDMI (or USB/I2S if you’re that way inclined). microSD only , with the same 1.8V signalling support as the Model B for the faster UHS card modes. External antenna support. This is the one I find most interesting. There are two antenna control lines (ANT_CTRL1 and ANT_CTRL2) and overlay parameters named ant1 , ant2 and noant , which is exactly how the Compute Module 4 switches between its onboard antenna and an external U.FL connector. If that carries over to the final board, it’d be a lovely addition for anyone sticking a Pi in a metal enclosure. PWR and ACT LEDs , the same SPI flash bootloader setup as the Model B, and the same power button definition as the Zero 3 W. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about USB. On the Model B, the USB 3 ports made use of the PCIe bus, and the PCIe controller is enabled here too, so USB 3 is possible, but the 3 Model A+ only had a single USB-A port and I’d probably expect the same here. The previous Model A, the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A from 2017 How Do They Compare? Here’s a quick side-by-side of what the device trees tell us, with the Pi 4 Model B thrown in for good measure. Anything marked with an asterisk is my interpretation of the device tree rather than something it states outright. Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W Raspberry Pi 4 Model A Raspberry Pi 4 Model B SoC Broadcom BCM2711 Broadcom BCM2711 Broadcom BCM2711 CPU Quad-core Cortex-A72 Quad-core Cortex-A72 Quad-core Cortex-A72 HDMI 1x 1x 2x micro HDMI Ethernet No No Gigabit Wi-Fi/Bluetooth Yes Yes, with antenna switching* Yes Storage microSD (unless..) microSD microSD Analogue Audio/Composite No No Yes (3.5mm) SPI Flash Bootloader Yes* Yes* Yes Power Button Yes* Yes* No LEDs ACT PWR, ACT PWR, ACT What We Don’t Know (Yet) Quite a lot, I’m afraid. Device trees don’t describe RAM, so there’s no word on memory configurations, and there’s nothing on pricing, clock speeds, connector types or a release date either. Pricing is the big one for me. Memory costs haven’t exactly been kind lately (I covered the last round of increases alongside the 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 launch ), and a lower-cost Pi 4 variant makes a lot of sense in that context. The BCM2711 is a mature chip at this point, it’s well supported in software, and a cut-down board gives people who don’t need a Pi 5 something cheaper to reach for. The Zero 3 W is a tougher one to call though, as the Zero range has always lived and died by its price, and I can’t imagine the BCM2711 being as cheap to build around as the RP3A0. Thoughts On the whole, I like what I’m seeing here. The Zero 3 W looks like the upgrade a lot of people have been asking for since the Zero 2 W landed, and the 4 Model A feels like a sensible way of squeezing more life out of the Pi 4 platform at a time when components aren’t getting any cheaper. The external antenna support on the 4 Model A is a really nice touch if it makes it to the final board. Saying that, everything above comes from device tree files rather than an official spec sheet, so mileage may vary when the real thing turns up. Kernel support landing ahead of launch is usually a good sign that it’s not far off, and you can bet I’ll be throwing both the Zero 3 W and the 4 Model A onto sbc.compare as soon as I can get one in my hands. Which of the two are you more excited about? Do let me know in the comments! Owners bring it up more in 13 of the 14; tennis ball machines are the exception, with only 91 owner opinions. 6,900 opinions from YouTube reviews and 3,567 from Reddit threads. Left out: video doorbells, smart thermostats, mechanical keyboards and 3D scanners, where reliability isn't a topic of its own (it's folded into a broader one such as "Connection, Reliability & Support") , and pickleball machines, which have no Reddit threads yet. Most of what breaks shows up after the review is done Robot vacuums: reliability comes up in 1% of reviewer opinions and 18% of owner opinions. A review covers a few weeks; the failures owners write about tend to come months later. Self-cleaning litter boxes: 3% vs 39% . Owners mostly describe breakdowns and how long a replacement takes. When owners do bring it up, 70% of what they say is negative. Reviewers who mention it are negative 15% of the time. Apps: the same attention, the opposite verdict Reviewers and owners talk about apps, software and connectivity about equally often ( 8.2% vs 9.4% of opinions). They don't agree on them: 21% of reviewer opinions on apps are negative, compared with 71% of owner opinions. Apps, software and connectivity: share of opinions that are negative Reviewers (YouTube) Owners (Reddit) Mechanical keyboards Reviewers 17% · owners 75% Smart locks Reviewers 17% · owners 72% Portable power stations Reviewers 15% · owners 69% 3D scanners Reviewers 28% · owners 72% Robot vacuums Reviewers 9% · owners 50% Smart rings Reviewers 42% · owners 75% Smart glasses Reviewers 38% · owners 71% 3D printers Reviewers 61% · owners 85% 0% 25% 50% 75% 100% Categories with at least 20 positive or negative owner opinions on apps. Owners are more negative in all eight. Two products show where this ends up: A $7,999 laser engraver ranks last of 9 . The Glowforge Pro gets 8 positive and 0 negative opinions on setup and ease of use. It loses on software and connectivity ( 3 positive, 7 negative ) and on reliability and support (2 positive, 7 negative) . Owners mostly object to a paid software subscription and needing an internet connection to use the machine. A $350 smart lock ranks last of 20 . The Eufy FamiLock S3 has 0 positive and 7 negative opinions on its app and smart-home features, mostly about a firmware update that left locks unusable. All 10 of its sources are Reddit threads. If you're about to buy Search owner threads for the model plus "months" or "a year later", not just the launch reviews. Check whether the device still works if the app or the company's servers go away. Look at the warranty length and how owners describe getting a replacement. Read this before the numbers Reviewers aren't hiding anything. Most reviews are made in the first days or weeks with a new unit. That's too early for most failures, and it's hard to test a company's support. Owners post when something goes wrong. Nobody starts a thread to say their robot vacuum still works, so these numbers show what owners worry about, not how often things break. For scale: across all topics, 56% of owner opinions and 15% of reviewer opinions are negative. Reliability ( 70% ) and apps ( 71% ) are still well above the owners' own average. Topic grouping matters. If we also count mixed topics such as "Value & Support" or "Responsiveness & Key Reliability", owners bring up reliability 2.4 times as often instead of twice , and more in all 17 categories that have owner opinions . We lead with the stricter number. The same goes for apps: mixed topics like "Connectivity & Battery" are left out. Some YouTube reviews are sponsored. We count them like any other source and can't reliably tell which ones are. An AI model labels each opinion with a topic and as positive or negative. Every opinion links back to the sentence it came from, so any of them can be checked. Method Sources: YouTube reviews and Reddit threads about 657 products currently on sale in 19 categories, collected for BettaScore's rankings: 8,062 opinions from YouTube and 4,525 from Reddit. Review sites, forums and Hacker News ( 517 opinions) aren't in the comparison. What counts as an opinion: one source's view on one topic of one product. A source that covers five topics counts five times; a source that mentions a topic ten times counts once. Topic groups: reliability is any topic about reliability, durability, warranty, service or support; apps is any topic about apps, software, firmware or connectivity. Mixed topics are left out of both. Shares: opinions in a topic group ÷ all opinions from that platform, including neutral ones. Negative shares count positive and negative opinions only. title: Hex Raises $100M
abstract:
Blog A new era for Hex, and data Announcing Hex 4.0, and a $100m fundraise — building toward the agent-native future for analytics. Barry McCardel Company October 27, 2026 Share: twitter linkedin A few months ago, after we had just closed our best-ever quarter, we decided to do something bold: start from scratch on a clean-sheet version of Hex, the product we had been building for 6 years and used by over 2,500 customers globally. This was a radical thing to do, but after 4 years on the frontier of bringing AI to data, we knew it was the right one. Today we’re introducing that new version — and announcing a fundraising to bring it to the world. Let me tell you why, and where we see all of this going. “What would we build if we were starting from scratch?”… and then doing it This was the question we asked ourselves earlier this year. See, we were founded in 2019, making us a pre-AI company (ew!). Now, I also think we had done an amazing job bringing AI into our product over those years. We had a text-to-SQL prototype using GPT-3 before ChatGPT. We launched our Magic features in February 2023. We built the first really good data agent last year, and earlier this year we changed the game again with generative apps . A lot to be proud of. But fundamentally, we were trying to integrate AI into a product that already existed . Our data model, architecture, and core assumptions around what users were doing in our product were all baked in 2020 to 2021 — we were far from “agent native”, no matter how much we liked saying it. ¹ And this was leading to some major issues: our agent harness was becoming bloated with hundreds of tools, which were required to teach agents about how to use Hex. External agent workflows felt clunky, because they were having to use Hex through a keyhole via MCP versus being able to work with something more native. And our compute engine wasn’t built to support the high-speed, high-concurrency, iterative workflows agents seem to like. In parallel, our customers were experiencing new challenges: primarily a data sprawl from analytics work happening in a lot of other places. Folks are using Cursor, Codex, Cognition, Claude, and custom agents, "vibe coding" dashboards and reports, and sharing the results as HTML files. They’re working around their legacy BI tools, and working without permissions, provenance, context, or observability. It’s a mess, but the previous version of Hex couldn’t solve this in the way we wanted. Altogether, this added to a growing sense that – despite growing quickly and having a lot of happy customers – we were headed for a point of diminishing returns with this approach. As we got together and talked about this, we formed of an idea of what we would build if we were starting from scratch today: a platform rooted in code — with all of its infinite flexibility and agent-nativity — but with the context, controls, guidance, and guardrails to make it trusted, no matter where it’s happening. And so that’s what we built. Introducing Hex 4.0 Hex 4.0 is truly a from-scratch rewrite for the era of agents ² . The core assumption of 4.0 is that everything is code — and that teams need context, controls, and compounding to make it trusted and scalable. It leans into the idea that data work is happening in a lot of places, and that "plain code" (not a proprietary YAML format) is the way to make that make sense. We have a big, long blog post detailing all of this here , I recommend you read it! Maybe a couple of times, because it's interesting, and we suspect you’re going to be hearing from a lot of other companies who are going to realize that they need to think from first principles too. And this is just the foundation for a lot of other things we have in mind ; in fact, one of the reasons we went so hard on this is because there are things we want to build we couldn't imagine doing on the old architecture — but are trivial on the new one. We can't wait to show you! Some money stuff: we raised another $100m As this all came into focus, we realized more money would help us go faster – to scale our team, expand go-to-market, and continue to make great swag. The only problem was that in the first part of the year, investors thought all software was going to die and there would only be two companies left. ³ Shailendra and the team at Peak XV, however, didn't think that: in fact, they were pretty sure that model-independent platforms were going to have a bright future ahead. And they were not scared about backing us taking a slightly crazy, first-principles approach to go build it. So I’m excited to announce that we’ve closed a $100 million financing round at a $1.2B valuation led by PeakXV and 137 Ventures, with participation from Amplify, Avra, a16z, Next Legacy, Redpoint, Sequoia, and Zero Prime. This gives us a bunch more runway to keep building this thing, and take more bold bets into the future. The end of BI, the beginning of something new I'm throwing some serious shade at the "SaaS apocalypse"-pilled investors above, but I'll give them some credit: it is true that a lot of software categories will effectively die over the next couple of years. But I also believe many of them will combine and be reborn into new shapes. This is our basic outlook on BI: the old paradigm is over, and no amount of bolting a chatbot sidebar onto the legacy platforms is going to change that. Agents don’t want to use the bespoke UI you wrote, and they don’t care about your esoteric data model. But these currents are also opening up fantastic new opportunities! The basic promise of BI is finally here: everyone can ask questions! Everyone can build! But now it's chaotic, and all the trust is gone. We see this as the core trade-off to break, and we're kind of obsessed with it. We believe the next chapter of data work is rooted in code, with the context and controls needed to establish trust, governance, and guardrails. And we’re so excited to show you what we have coming next. ¹ I'm not going to call out anyone by name, but I do think it's funny how many companies in our space that have been around for 5 years or more now call themselves "AI native", despite that literally being the antithesis of that phrase. I mean, I get why they're doing it, but unless you have literally rebuilt your product in the last 24 months, I'm not sure you can credibly claim it... ² And, of course, was greatly accelerated by using agents to write all of the code, guided by the decades of combined expertise from our teams in building scaled data platforms. ³ I'm joking, but not really? You should have sat in some of the pitch meetings we had… Share: twitter linkedin This is something we think a lot about at Hex, where we're creating a platform that makes it easy to build and share interactive data products which can help teams be more impactful. title: Evidence of a spying operation by ICE against left-wing social movements
abstract:
Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond. The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities. Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s. Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 . Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown. Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s. Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025. Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area. Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order. The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them. Their defense attorneys say the heavy charges filed against the Minnesota 15 don’t align with their alleged conduct. “This is the first time I’ve had a client who’s accused of a conspiracy and went on a speaking tour,” says Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant. Peeking Through the Keyhole An internal ICE document laying out the scope of Operation Puppet Master—which led to the indictment of the Minneapolis 15—ends by noting, “This case has also been accepted under CUC Op Keyhole.” According to prosecutors , Operation Keyhole is a long-standing program created by HSI’s Saint Paul office to fund “undercover activity”—primarily equipment purchases and personnel costs—in a region covering Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska. The program has funded at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it started in December 2008. The CUC prefix, per an internal 2008 DHS handbook unearthed by the independent media outlet Unicorn Riot , refers to Certified Undercover Operations, a formal designation with clearly defined oversight mechanisms, procedures, and reporting requirements. Operation Keyhole’s parameters are reviewed every six months by a committee comprising senior DOJ and DHS officials. As of June 2026, when it was last renewed, Keyhole funded six active investigations, including Project Whipple Shield, which was initiated in February to probe claims of assault, stalking, and doxing of DHS agents and other federal employees, and underpins the Minnesota 15 indictment. At least 11 undercover agents working under Operation Keyhole infiltrated Twin Cities anti-ICE activists, participating in martial arts and know-your-rights trainings, marches, general strikes, and community meetings. They also infiltrated activists’ communications network for identifying possible undercover ICE vehicles and dispatching activists to tail them through the Twin Cities, and penetrated several activist group chats on Signal, transmitting their contents back to other HSI colleagues for analysis and eventual inclusion in the indictment. Activist conferences as far away as Seattle, Michigan, Chicago , and New York City were placed under surveillance as part of the investigation, and HSI teams photographed and ran the license plates of every car parked in the lot of a meeting location or seen transporting activists. There is also drone footage from unarmed Customs and Border Protection Reaper drones of the activists moving around the Twin Cities area. The undercovers were part of a much broader group of more than 50 HSI agents, including at least two dozen from HSI’s little-known Special Operations Group, that took part in the investigation and surveillance of the defendants, both digital and in-person. Feds with decades of experience on complex financial crimes, drug cartel investigations, human trafficking, and organized crime were pulled into the Minnesota 15 investigation. Several of the Minnesota 15 case agents are from out of state and appear in court records for the prosecutions of anti-ICE activists in other cities. This includes Los Angeles–based HSI agents Robert Kurtz III , who specializes in financial fraud, and Ryan Ribner, who allegedly assaulted SEIU California president David Huerta at a June 2025 protest of an ICE enforcement operation, arrested him, and then claimed the then 58-year-old Huerta attacked federal law enforcement. (Huerta’s charges were dropped in July after videos contradicting Ribner’s account surfaced.) HSI records show Ribner was also involved in at least two prosecutions of Southern California residents who physically confronted ICE and Border Patrol agents last year. Other agents from the conspiracy investigation have also been involved in recent high-profile incidents. Tim Gerber, the “team leader” of an HSI Special Operations Group squad, led the investigation of former CNN host Don Lemon for reporting on a protest at a Minneapolis Church where an ICE agent was a pastor.

title: The Agent SDK
abstract:
Software teams use agents defined as code to handle recurring work across the development lifecycle. These agents connect to the places where a team works and act when relevant events occur, whether that means reviewing a pull request, executing a compliance workflow, or investigating an incident. The most useful agents are tailored to how a particular team operates. Until now, building one has generally meant adopting a product designed around someone else's workflow or starting from scratch. Today, we're releasing the Agent SDK, the framework we use to build our own managed agents like Bugbot, Security Reviewer, and Rollouts. Agent SDK allows you to define agents in code and manage them like any other software project. Start from a template or point your coding agent at our docs. When the agent is ready, agent-sdk deploy it to Cursor infrastructure with one command. # Build around your workflow The Agent SDK lets you quickly build and deploy agents that work the way your team does. They respond to the events your team already handles and follow policies your team can inspect and change. Code review is one example. Each team has its own standards for what requires attention and who should review it. With the Agent SDK, you can build an agent that responds to pull request events from GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The agent can assess the risk of a change, route it to the right team, and approve changes that meet your policy. As an example, a team within Cursor had built a large, fast-growing knowledge base of lessons learned and wanted every pull request checked against it. This way, the team's past decisions would hold even as the codebase changed. With the Agent SDK, they built kb-reviewer in about a day. It now runs on every PR in their main codebase, flags changes that contradict a recorded lesson, cites the note behind each finding, and encourages engineers to reconcile the discrepancies it reports. For more complicated work, agents can hand a task to another specialized agent with its own tools and sessions. They can also divide a job among subagents working in parallel. The Agent SDK also supports evals and event replay out of the box, allowing for rapid development with assurances that critical workflows execute the way you expect. The PGA Tour uses the Agent SDK to power their software development factory. Evals keep them moving quickly. The Agent SDK has enabled PGA to build every component of our software factory on Cursor's infrastructure. It provides the flexibility we need to build agents that drive our development process. And built-in support for evals allows us to quickly iterate on new ideas and optimize existing capabilities reliably. Michael Gyarmathy Principal Engineer , PGA America # Define everything in code An Agent SDK agent is organized like a small software project. The instructions that guide it sit alongside code for its tools, connections to outside services, and the evals used to test it. Each file represents something the agent knows or can do. Prompts are written in Markdown, while tools are defined as TypeScript functions. Because everything is code, changes can go through the same version control and review process as the rest of your software. # Deploy agents wherever you need them When you're ready to put an agent into use, you can deploy it to Cursor by running agent-sdk deploy from the project directory. The command builds the agent, gives it a URL, and starts it on our infrastructure. You can manage secrets and integrations from the dashboard, while continuing to use the same logs, evals, and playground available locally. You can also run the agent on your own infrastructure. Each agent runs as a single Node process that can be packaged in a container. # Get started Getting started with the Agent SDK looks much like starting any other software project. Create a project directory, then launch the local playground: import { homedir } from "node:os" ; import { join } from "node:path" ; import { defineAgent } from "@cursor/agent-sdk" ; export default defineAgent ({ name: "Robo" , model: { id: "composer-2.5" , params: [ { id: "effort" , value: "high" }, { id: "fast" , value: "true" }, ], }, local: { cwd: join ( homedir (), ".cache" , "factory" , "robo" ), }, }) From there, you can iterate locally and run evals before deploying with agent-sdk deploy . The Agent SDK also ships with skills that guide coding agents through the development process. You can point an agent at the docs and have it help build the bot with you. The Agent SDK is generally available today. Read the docs and get started.

title: Mossad Has Devices Like the Exploding Pagers in "Every Country You Can Imagine" (2025)
abstract:
Former Mossad Chief Yossi Cohen: Planted Devices Like The Exploding Hezbollah Pagers Are In “Every Country You Can Imagine” October 24, 2025 11:50 am 3 Comments Netanyahu with former Mossad head Yossi Cohen. (Photo: GPO) Former Mossad director Yossi Cohen has offered an account of his agency’s global intelligence operations–revealing that the widely-publicized sabotage of Hezbollah’s communications infrastructure in September 2024 is only part of a far broader espionage campaign. In an appearance on the The Brink podcast, Cohen said the now-notorious “pager operation” — in which operatives within Hezbollah were duped into activating explosive-laden devices — reflected a strategic paradigm he developed more than two decades ago. The method, he said, is known within Mossad as the “manipulated equipment method” or “pager method,” and it was implemented across “virtually every potential theatre of operation.” “You know how many equipment I mean treated equipment that we have in these countries? You can’t. You don’t. I do,” Cohen said of the scale of the campaign. “In all the countries that you can imagine,” he added when pressed for geographic specifics. Cohen traced the origins of the scheme to the early 2000s, saying it was developed in the period 2002-2004 while he led Mossad’s Special Operations division under former chief Meir Dagan. According to Cohen, the logic was simple: if adversaries are purchasing equipment, Israel should intervene by embedding itself into their supply chain and exploiting it. “If I know that … Iran or other countries … are buying something that I can be part of their supply chain, I will do,” Cohen said. He pointed to the 2006 Second Lebanon War — in which Israel fought Hezbollah — as the initial battlefield where this “manipulated equipment” tactic was tested. Cohen says that the strategic method was then scaled and refined for global use. Perhaps most striking, Cohen admitted that the system had not been deployed effectively in the Gaza Strip, identifying the region as a “critical shortfall” in Mossad’s intelligence architecture. “Not Gaza. Not enough,” he told the podcast host. He suggested that had the system been operational there, Israel’s readiness in the run-up to the October 7th 2023 attack might have been very different. Cohen didn’t restrict his critique to foreign targets. He also took aim at Israel’s internal security agencies. He said that when he sought to take responsibility for intelligence operations in Gaza prior to the October 7 attack, he was met with stiff resistance from both Shin Bet (Israel’s internal security service) and the IDF Intelligence Directorate. Cohen claimed the agencies treated Mossad’s proposals with institutional arrogance: “We’re the IDF… we’re Shin Bet… we don’t need you.” He maintained that his warnings about a deficiency in intelligence coverage were regularly voiced, but went unheeded: “I have told and written that they ‘have nothing sufficient on the level of intelligence’ prior to October 7th.” And he challenged those agencies for failing to publicly dispute the claim. The revelations raise fundamental questions about how far Israel’s covert operations have extended–and where vulnerabilities remain. By describing a system that is global, meticulously engineered and highly embedded in adversary logistics, Cohen’s account sheds light on the evolving nature of intelligence warfare in the 21st century. But the admission of a gap in Gaza may fuel renewed scrutiny of Israel’s strategic posture along its southern border. Critics may argue that if Mossad’s capabilities were so advanced elsewhere, why were they unable–or perhaps unpermitted–to deploy them where they were arguably most needed. title: Comparative Analysis of Transformer-Based Models for Question Answering on SQuAD v2.0
abstract: Transformer-based architectures have revolutionized Question Answering (QA), yet navigating the trade-off between architectural complexity, computational efficiency, and robust generalization remains a critical challenge. This study presents a rigorous, side-by-side evaluation of four distinct Transformer models—ALBERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and XLNet—on the SQuAD v2.0 benchmark, which demands both precise span extraction and calibration to abstain from unanswerable queries. By employing identical preprocessing pipelines and hyperparameter schedules, we isolate the impact of specific architectural innovations, including dynamic masking, disentangled attention, and permutation language modeling. Experimental results establish RoBERTa as the performance leader (85.90% EM, 88.69% F1), validating the efficacy of robust optimization strategies. Notably, DeBERTa followed closely (85.41% EM, 88.54% F1) but achieved superior performance on unanswerable questions (88.24%), suggesting that its disentangled attention mechanism offers enhanced verification capabilities against distractor entities. XLNet demonstrated competitive potential (78.30% EM) via its autoregressive formulation, while ALBERT confirmed its status as the efficiency benchmark, delivering respectable accuracy (80.70% EM) with a fraction of the parameter footprint. Qualitative error analysis reveals that while lighter models are prone to "hallucinating" answers, advanced architectures primarily fail due to subtle reasoning errors rather than entity mismatch. These findings provide a definitive decision framework for practitioners: prioritizing RoBERTa and DeBERTa for maximum reliability in complex domains, and leveraging ALBERT for scalable, resource-constrained deployments.

title: Editorial
abstract:
Dear Readers,
 I am very pleased to announce today the eleventh J.UCS issue of 2026. In this issue, various topical aspects of computer science are covered in 5 articles by 10 authors from 4 countries (Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Türkiye). As always, I would like to thank all the authors for their sound research and the editorial board for their highly valuable review effort and suggestions for improvement. These contributions sustain the quality of our journal. I would also like to express my sincere thanks to the KOALA Initiative and its team for their financial support, without which the J.UCS team would not be able to publish our journal.
 In an ongoing effort to further strengthen our journal, we are highly interested in receiving high-quality proposals for special issues on new topics and trends. Please consider yourself and encourage your colleagues to submit high-quality articles or special issue proposals for our journal.
 In this regular issue, I am very pleased to introduce the following 5 accepted articles:
 Fagner Leal Pantoja, André Santanchè, and Claudia Bauzer Medeiros from Brazil investigate in their research whether topic models are effective tools for capturing the semantic content of datasets. The results suggest that the topics are effective in representing the main themes of the input datasets. However, some discrepancies remain between automatic evaluation metrics and human interpretation. This supports the view that language models cannot fully capture semantic meaning, as communicative intent (an essential aspect of semantics) may lie outside the training data.
 In a collaborative research between Indonesia and Taiwan, Army Justitia and Hei-Chia Wang propose in their article SciRelate, an enhanced framework for related work generation. SciRelate is capable of grouping scientific articles using a clustering method, performing abstractive summarization on these groups, and generating subsection headings that represent their topic. The results show that LDA effectively clusters referenced papers, BART-large-CNN performs the strong Related Work generation, and the proposed TopicFusion-MP consistently outperforms existing keyword extraction models for subsection headings.
 Cristiano Welter and Kleinner Farias from Brazil focus in their research on the problem that developing Cloud-of-Things (CoT) applications remains challenging due to heterogeneous technologies and complex deployment requirements. To address these challenges, the article introduces Model of Things (MoT), a model-driven, low-code approach that integrates UML modeling, automated model transformations, and application deployment. A case study demonstrated MoT's feasibility in generating executable CoT applications, while an evaluation involving 12 participants revealed positive perceptions of its usefulness and ease of use.
 Oğuzhan Kırlar and Mehmet Ali Altuncu from Türkiye focus in their work on transformer-based question answering. The article compares ALBERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and XLNet on SQuAD v2.0 to examine their performance, efficiency, and ability to handle unanswerable questions under the same training conditions. The results show that RoBERTa gives the best overall performance, DeBERTa performs best on unanswerable questions, and ALBERT is a suitable option for resource-constrained environments.
 And last but not least, Cuneyt Ozdemir from Türkiye focuses on the problem of objective pain assessment which remains challenging due to the subjective nature of pain and inter-subject variability. Therefore, the article proposes a hybrid deep-learning architecture that combines single-channel EEG band-power streams with wrist-worn peripheral biosignals (electrodermal activity, BVP, accelerometry, and skin temperature) using residual 1D-CNN and MLP encoders, aiming to classify four natural pain phenotypes: headache, low back pain, menstrual pain, and no pain. Under a strict subject-wise evaluation protocol on PhysioPain, the model reaches 86.98% accuracy and 87.46% weighted F1 at a latency of about 0.15 ms per sample, outperforming classical machine-learning baselines as well as DenseNet-1D and ResNet-1D, and representing a step toward generalizable, real-time pain-related digital biomarkers.
 Enjoy Reading!
 Best regards,
 Christian Gütl, Managing Editor-in-Chief
 Graz University of Technology, Graz, Austria

title: Efficacy and Mechanism of Generative AI in Empowering English Writing Instruction
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence technology brings new transformative opportunities to English writing instruction. This paper analyzes the efficacy and mechanism of generative AI in empowering English writing teaching. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and Self-Regulated Learning theory, it summarizes teaching efficacy from three dimensions—the quality of writing output, cognitive support during the writing process, and real-time adaptation of writing feedback—and further reveals the underlying mechanism through three layers: cognitive load reduction, learning motivation activation, and metacognitive strategy activation. Using data from a 12-week quasi-experimental study, it compares the experimental and control groups in terms of writing performance, writing strategy use, and feedback engagement. The results show that generative AI-assisted instruction has a moderately strong facilitative effect on learners' writing performance, achieved mainly by reducing extraneous cognitive load, enhancing writing self-efficacy, and deepening feedback engagement. This study provides theoretical grounding and practical reference for integrating generative AI into the English writing classroom.
